Say the table aloud once. Later slides reuse these symbols and do not switch to other letters for the response. The three GLMs share one skeleton. Five sketches come next, then the algebra panels, then the spread of \(Y\) versus the spread of \(\bar Y\).

title: From the question to the model
section: \(Y\) is the response, \(x\) is the covariate
text:
\(Y\) is the response, \(x\) is the covariate



One observational row: a covariate cell marked x beside a response cell marked Y.


One row of the data holds both. \(Y\) is what the model describes. \(x\) is what it conditions on.

Point at the two cells, not at a dataset yet. Ask which column in their own table is \(Y\). The answer should be the measurement, not the treatment or the depth.

title: From the question to the model
text:
\(\mu\) is the conditional mean



At one value of x, several responses Y scatter around a mark labelled mu.








Model


\(\mu = \mathbb{E}(Y \mid x)\)



The dots are possible values of \(Y\) at that \(x\). \(\mu\) is their mean, not one of the dots.

The slice is one \(x\). \(\mu\) sits in the middle of the \(Y\)s. The usual misreading is to treat \(\mu\) as a fitted line already; the line comes on the next slide.
Going further. \(\mu(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbb{E}(Y \mid \mathbf{x})\) is the function \(m\) that minimises the expected squared error \(\mathbb{E}\{(Y - m(\mathbf{x}))^2\}\); geometrically it is the \(L^2\) projection of \(Y\) onto functions of \(\mathbf{x}\). Change the loss and the target changes: absolute error gives the conditional median, and the check loss gives a conditional quantile. That is why “regression” without a named target is ambiguous for skewed responses. The conditional mean exists only when \(\mathbb{E}|Y| < \infty\). A standard treatment is in Rice, Mathematical Statistics and Data Analysis (Rice, n.d.).

title: From the question to the model
section: The identity link leaves \(\mu\) on its own scale
text:
The identity link leaves \(\mu\) on its own scale



A straight line of mu against x.








Model


\(g(\mu) = \mu = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x\)



A Gaussian linear model is this case. \(\beta_1\) is a change in the mean of \(Y\), in the units of \(Y\).

The line is \(\mu\), not a cloud of observations. Identity means \(g\) does nothing. \(\beta_1\) keeps the units of \(Y\).
Going further. The identity is the canonical link of the Gaussian family, so ordinary least squares and maximum likelihood coincide when \(Y \mid \mathbf{x} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)\). Normality is not needed for the point estimate: the Gauss–Markov theorem makes \(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}\) the best linear unbiased estimator as soon as the errors have mean zero, constant variance, and no correlation. Normality buys exact \(t\) and \(F\) distributions in small samples. The identity link can predict a negative mean, which is the first warning sign for counts and concentrations. See Agresti, Foundations of Linear and Generalized Linear Models (Agresti 2015).

title: From the question to the model
text:
Log and logit move \(\mu\) first



A log-mean curve of mu against x, and a logit curve of pi against x.










Model


\(\log \mu = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x\)










Model


\(\mathrm{logit}(\pi) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x\)




On the log link, a step of 1 in \(x\) multiplies \(\mu\) by \(\exp(\beta_1)\). On the logit, \(Y\) is binary, so \(\mu = \pi\), and the same step multiplies the odds by \(\exp(\beta_1)\).

Left curve is a count mean, right curve is a probability. Both still have the same linear predictor. Ask which of their responses is a count and which is a detection.
Going further. Log and logit are the canonical links of the Poisson and Bernoulli families: writing the density in exponential-family form, the natural parameter is \(g(\mu)\), so \(\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{y}\) is sufficient and the score equations reduce to \(\mathbf{X}^{\top}(\mathbf{y} - \boldsymbol\mu) = 0\). The fit uses iteratively reweighted least squares. \(\exp(\beta_1)\) is a rate ratio on the log link and an odds ratio on the logit. The odds ratio is non-collapsible: adding a covariate that is unrelated to \(x\) still changes \(\beta_1\), unlike a risk difference. Agresti’s Foundations of Linear and Generalized Linear Models covers both links (Agresti 2015).

title: From the question to the model
text:
\(i\) sits inside \(j\)



Three observations labelled i inside one cluster labelled j.


\(j\) is the cluster the treatment sits on: a site, an enclosure, a batch. \(i\) is one row inside it: a core, a date, a collar. Rows that share a \(j\) are not independent replicates.

Point at \(j\) first, then the three \(i\)s. Ask which index received the treatment in their design. If they say the core, the enclosure is the \(j\) they have skipped.
Going further. With a cluster effect \(u_j \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_u^2)\) and residual variance \(\sigma^2\), two rows in the same \(j\) have intraclass correlation \(\rho = \sigma_u^2 / (\sigma_u^2 + \sigma^2)\). For a cluster-level treatment with \(m\) rows per cluster, the variance of a mean is inflated by the design effect \(1 + (m - 1)\rho\), so the effective sample size is \(n / \{1 + (m-1)\rho\}\). As \(\rho \to 1\), it tends to the number of clusters. Treating the \(i\) as independent is what Hurlbert named pseudoreplication (📄 Pseudoreplication and the design of ecological field experiments, Ecological Monographs, 1984).

title: From the question to the model
text:
The hat matrix



Panel 4: the projection matrix onto the column space of X.


\(P_X\) projects \(y\) onto the column space. When \(X\) has full column rank, \(P_X = X(X^{\mathsf T}X)^{-1}X^{\mathsf T}\), and \(\hat y = P_X y\).

The hat matrix name is deliberate: \(\hat y\) is a linear function of \(y\). Mention rank only if someone asks about collinearity.
Going further. \(P_X\) is symmetric and idempotent, with trace equal to its rank \(p\), the number of columns. Its diagonal \(h_{ii}\) is the leverage of row \(i\): it averages \(p/n\), and \(\mathrm{Var}(y_i - \hat y_i) = \sigma^2 (1 - h_{ii})\), which is why raw residuals are studentised before they are compared. Cook’s distance combines \(h_{ii}\) with the residual. In a GLM the same role is played by \(\mathbf{W}^{1/2}\mathbf{X}(\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{W}\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{W}^{1/2}\), with \(\mathbf{W}\) the IRLS weights at convergence.

title: From the question to the model
text:
Two spreads, not one


Empirical
\[
s = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(Y_i - \bar Y)^2}
\]
\(s\) is the spread of the observations around \(\bar Y\). The empirical standard error of the mean replaces the unknown scale with that \(s\):
\[
\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}
\]

Theoretical
The estimand here is the mean. Its sampling variance is \(\sigma^2/n\), so
\[
\mathrm{SE}(\bar Y) = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}.
\]
In the draw on the next slides, \(\sigma = 15\) and \(n = 50\), so \(15/\sqrt{50} = 2.12\). The standard deviation of the 1,000 means is 2.11.


Read both formulas once. The common mistake is reporting \(s\) where the reader expects an uncertainty for \(\bar Y\). Ask the room which number would go in an error bar for the mean.
Going further. \(\mathrm{Var}(\bar Y) = \sigma^2/n\) needs the \(Y_i\) to be uncorrelated with a common variance; with clustered rows it is multiplied by the design effect. \(s^2\) is unbiased for \(\sigma^2\), but \(s\) is slightly biased for \(\sigma\) (Jensen’s inequality). Under normality \((\bar Y - \mu)/(s/\sqrt{n})\) follows a \(t_{n-1}\) distribution exactly; otherwise the central limit theorem makes it approximately standard normal for large \(n\), at a rate that worsens with skewness. See Hogg, McKean and Craig (Hogg et al. 2019).

Multivariable is not multivariate



Diagram contrasting multivariable regression, one outcome with several predictors, and multivariate analysis, several outcomes modelled jointly.


Timothy Achala drew the distinction this way. Click the figure if the type is small. The wording we will police is say the precise word.

One \(Y\) versus several correlated outcomes: let the diagram do the work. Ask who has seen “multivariate logistic” in a paper title when the authors meant several predictors.

title: From the question to the model
text:
Variance and uncertainty


How variable is a quantity or estimator?
\[
\mathrm{Var}(X), \quad \mathrm{Var}(\hat{\theta})
\]
Variance measures dispersion, not bias or distance to truth.



Standard errors
Confidence intervals
Hypothesis tests
Uncertainty quantification

Uncertainty is information about precision, not a problem to eliminate.

The standard deviation and the standard error are the two scales that sentence has to keep apart.

Return to the histogram pair if the room conflates \(s\) and SE. Bias versus variance is not on the strip; do not improvise a lecture here.
Going further. Mean squared error splits as \(\mathbb{E}(\hat\theta - \theta)^2 = \mathrm{Var}(\hat\theta) + \{\mathbb{E}(\hat\theta) - \theta\}^2\), so a low-variance estimator can still be far from the truth. Among unbiased estimators, the Cramér–Rao bound \(\mathrm{Var}(\hat\theta) \ge 1/I(\theta)\) holds under regularity conditions: the support does not depend on \(\theta\) and differentiation passes under the integral. Shrinkage, penalised smoothing, and priors trade a little bias for a larger cut in variance. Hogg, McKean and Craig state the bound (Hogg et al. 2019).

title: From the question to the model
text:
CA-SYS soil bacteria 🔬
The count table for this workshop is the CA-SYS 16S survey (Klockenbring et al. 2026b).

120 ha of arable land at the Domaine d’Épiosses, near Dijon
Four pesticide-free cropping systems, sampled 2018–2021
42 plots, four subplots each; 640 samples, 595 after quality control
10,633 OTUs from 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing

Data and the analysis vignettes are public (Klockenbring et al. 2026a). The next slide is that record.

Two minutes. The headline is that this is a real count table with a real sampling design, not a tidy teaching matrix. The four systems are the treatment, the plot is the unit, the subplot is the repeat. Hold the statistics until the next slide. If someone asks why not NEON: the NEON soil-microbe product now requires an account for portal downloads and a token for the API, so it no longer satisfies “click a link and download”.

title: From the question to the model
text:
The zones are the design



Three zones: no-till with SD1 and SD2, mixed with both practices, and tilled with TS1 plus nitrogen and TS2 without it.


SD1 and SD2 are the no-till systems. TS1 and TS2 are tilled, and only TS1 adds exogenous nitrogen. The mixed zone is where both practices occur.

Use the picture to fix the two contrasts: tillage runs left to right, nitrogen is only the TS1 label. The mixed panel is why a tillage coefficient is not a clean comparison. One minute, then the code.

title: From the question to the model
text:
Reading the published object

ps <- readRDS("data/16s_RNA_sequencing/casys_phyloseq_clean.rds")

counts <- unclass(attributes(ps)$otu_table)   # 10,633 OTUs x 595 samples
taxonomy <- as.data.frame(unclass(attributes(ps)$tax_table))
meta <- as.data.frame(unclass(attributes(ps)$sam_data))

casys <- tibble(
  sample_id = colnames(counts),
  system = factor(meta$System, levels = c("SD1", "SD2", "TS1", "TS2")),
  year = as.integer(meta$Year),
  plot = meta$Parcelle,
  total_reads = colSums(counts),
  richness = colSums(counts > 0),
  nitrospira_reads = colSums(counts[taxonomy$Genus == "Nitrospira", ])
)

The deposit is a phyloseq object, built to be read with Bioconductor. This excerpt reads the same slots. prepare-teaching-data.R writes casys_teaching.csv and leaves the raw object untouched. Column meanings are in the dataset README.

Bioconductor’s phyloseq is the reader the object was made for: otu_table(), tax_table(), sample_data(). The excerpt reaches those slots without loading the package, so the deck still renders where Bioconductor is not installed. The script is the only place the teaching table is built. Offer the three download links if someone wants the files.

title: From the question to the model
text:
The teaching columns






Five rows at a time. Design, effort, and response are the three roles. The file behind the table is casys_teaching.csv.

Do not read every row. Show Design, then Effort, then Response, and say the colour is the role. Sequencing depth and total reads are both library sizes, and they are not the same number: one is the published depth, the other is recomputed after filtering. Richness, a taxon count, and a presence are the three responses on the next slide.

title: From the question to the model
text:
What \(Y\) is in that table
Three responses, three supports:

Reads for one taxon. A non-negative integer, with a sampling effort that differs between samples
Richness. The number of OTUs observed in a sample, an integer bounded by 10,633
Presence. Whether a taxon was seen at all, a 0/1 response

None of the three is a free Gaussian. The family that matches each is the family table.






Ask which of the three the room would have analysed with a t-test. The honest answer is usually a relative abundance, which is a fourth object again: a composition. Say that compositions are deliberately out of scope today and are on the what-next slides.
Going further. The support fixes the candidate families: \(\{0, 1, 2, \dots\}\) suggests Poisson or negative binomial, \(\{0, \dots, N\}\) with a known \(N\) suggests a binomial, and \(\{0, 1\}\) forces a Bernoulli, whose variance \(\pi(1 - \pi)\) is set by its mean. Richness is a count of a different kind: it depends on sequencing depth through the accumulation curve, and its expectation is not linear in depth, so an offset on log depth is only an approximation. Agresti’s Foundations of Linear and Generalized Linear Models sets out the families by support (Agresti 2015).

title: From the question to the model
section: Two facts about the count table
text:
Two facts about the count table



Left, a histogram of OTU prevalence: most OTUs appear in a small fraction of samples. Right, a histogram of library size per sample.


74.6% of entries are zero, and the library size runs from 11,123 to 85,010 reads. Both numbers come from generate-data-figures.R.

These two panels do most of the work for the GLM block. The zeros kill the Gaussian story. The unequal library sizes are why a raw taxon count cannot be compared across samples, and they are the reason the offset appears later. The 74.6% figure matches the published data descriptor, which is a useful check that the object was read correctly.

title: From the question to the model
text:
Sampling effort is a covariate


If sample A has twice the reads of sample B, it has about twice the chance of showing any given taxon, with no biology involved.






Model


\[
\log \mu_i = \mathbf{x}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta} + \log(\text{library size}_i)
\]



The last term is an offset: a column with a coefficient fixed at 1. The model is then about a rate per read, not a raw count. The fitted version is one mean, two variance assumptions.




This is the slide where a modelling idea comes from a property of the measurement rather than from a textbook. Note the offset is not a covariate whose coefficient is estimated. If someone asks about rarefying to a common depth instead: it throws away data and it does not remove the dependence, and the offset is the model-based alternative. Keep it short; the evidence is two slides later.
Going further. With exposure \(t_i\) (here the library size) and rate \(\lambda_i\), the model is \(Y_i \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(t_i \lambda_i)\) with \(\log \lambda_i = \mathbf{x}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol\beta\), which gives the displayed equation; \(\exp(\beta_k)\) is then a rate ratio per read. Replacing the offset by \(\log t_i\) as a covariate with a free coefficient tests proportionality: a coefficient far from 1 says that effort and counts are not proportional. Dividing the count by \(t_i\) and fitting a Gaussian model instead changes both the target and the variance structure. The same offset works unchanged in the negative binomial.

title: From the question to the model
section: Why a Gaussian lm is the wrong first tool
text:
Why a Gaussian lm is the wrong first tool

A count cannot be negative, and a Gaussian mean can predict a negative count
The variance of these counts rises with the mean, so one \(\sigma^2\) does not fit
A proportion is bounded, and a rise in one taxon is a fall in another’s share
Zeros are a property of community tables, not rows to delete

The evidence for the second line is on the mean against variance slide. The deep dive is after the pitfalls.

Going further. Each line is a statement about the variance function \(V(\mu)\): a Gaussian model fixes \(V(\mu) = 1\), a Poisson \(V(\mu) = \mu\), a binomial share \(V(\mu) = \mu(1 - \mu)/N\). Wedderburn’s quasi-likelihood (1974) shows that a mean model plus a correct \(V(\mu)\) is enough for consistent estimates and valid standard errors, without the full distribution. Transforming first, as \(\log(Y + 1)\), makes the result depend on the arbitrary constant and handles the zeros badly; O’Hara and Kotze compare the two approaches by simulation (📄 Do not log-transform count data, Methods in Ecology and Evolution, 2010).

title: From the question to the model
section: Mean against variance, for every OTU
text:
Mean against variance, for every OTU



Log-log scatter of per-OTU variance against per-OTU mean, with the line variance equals mean.


9,924 of 10,603 OTUs have a variance above their mean. A Poisson fixes those two quantities to be equal, which is the assumption the negative binomial relaxes.

This is the real version of the simulated mean-variance figure the deck used to show. Each point is one OTU: its mean across the 595 samples against its variance. The diagonal is the Poisson. Note honestly that a few hundred OTUs sit on or below the line, which is what you expect for the very rare ones where almost every count is zero.
Going further. A Poisson has variance function \(V(\mu) = \mu\). The negative binomial arises as a Poisson whose mean is itself gamma-distributed, giving \(V(\mu) = \mu + \mu^2/\theta\); quasi-Poisson keeps \(V(\mu) = \phi\mu\) and estimates \(\phi\) from the Pearson statistic \(\sum_i (y_i - \hat\mu_i)^2/\hat\mu_i\) divided by \(n - p\). The two make different predictions on this plot: a quadratic rise for the negative binomial, a line parallel to the diagonal for quasi-Poisson. Here each OTU’s variance also mixes samples of different depth and system, so part of the excess is unmodelled mean structure rather than biology.

title: From the question to the model
section: Four analyses, only one of them today
text:
Four analyses, only one of them today







Approach
What it targets




Compare proportions between systems
A share, with a false independence story


Poisson or negative binomial, with an offset
\(\mathbb{E}(Y \mid x)\) for a count, per read


Log-ratio (CLR and its relatives)
A composition, after the zeros are handled


Absolute against relative
Whether the taxon changed, or only its share



Today we fit the count models and the logit. Compositions return on the what-next slides.

This is the pedagogical contract. Do not start a CLR derivation. If pressed, say that a log-ratio needs a rule for the 74.6% zeros before any transformation, and that this rule is a scientific decision rather than a default.

text:
The hierarchy in the sampling

  y1["2021"] --> p1["Plot"]
  p0 --> u0["OTU counts"]

The cropping system is a property of the plot. Four subplots in one plot are not four independent trials of that system. 2018 was sampled before the treatments were applied, so it is a baseline rather than a treated year.

Two things to flag. The subplot point is the replication pitfall, three hours early; the design block returns to it as a random intercept on the plot. The baseline year matters because a naive model with year as a factor will happily report a 2018 “effect” of a treatment that did not exist yet. That is a design fact you can only get from the dataset documentation.
Going further. Hurlbert (📄 Pseudoreplication and the design of ecological field experiments, Ecological Monographs, 1984) defines pseudoreplication as testing a treatment effect with an error term taken from a level below the experimental unit. Here the system is assigned to the plot, so the denominator for the system contrast must come from plot-to-plot variation; a random intercept \(u_j\) on the plot does that. With a baseline, the usual efficient analysis adjusts the post-treatment response for the 2018 value (an ANCOVA-type model) rather than using change scores or a year factor.

title: From the question to the model
text:
SPRUCE 🌲
A whole-ecosystem warming experiment on the S1 bog, Marcell Experimental Forest, Minnesota.

Question on the design page: how do plants, microbes, and ecosystem processes respond to warming, and how does elevated \(\mathrm{CO}_2\) change that response?
Air and deep peat warmed from ambient to \(+9^\circ\mathrm{C}\)
Elevated \(\mathrm{CO}_2\) atmospheres of about 800–900 ppm
Source: SPRUCE experimental design

The next slide is that page.

All treatment numbers on the following slides are taken from that page, which cites Hanson et al. (2017) for the temperature differential and Cottingham et al. (2005) for regression designs. Do not expand those citations beyond what the page states. Two minutes. If the frame is blank, use the link.

title: From the question to the model
section: Ten enclosures, not a two-group test
text:
Ten enclosures, not a two-group test
Ambient and elevated \(\mathrm{CO}_2\), each at \(+0\), \(+2.25\), \(+4.5\), \(+6.75\), and \(+9^\circ\mathrm{C}\).

spruce |>
  distinct(plot, warming_c, co2, chambered) |>
  arrange(plot)
#> plots 4, 10, 11, 16, 19 are the elevated-CO2 enclosures
#> plots 7 and 21 are unchambered ambient plots, with no assigned warming

Twelve plots: ten chambered enclosures on the warming grid, and two ambient plots that were never assigned a level. The teaching table is spruce_teaching.csv, built by prepare-teaching-data.R from the published copy-number file.

Run the distinct() call in front of the room if the laptop allows. The point is that the design is recoverable from the data, and that the two ambient plots are a different kind of row: they have no warming level, so they cannot enter a regression on warming without a decision about what to do with them. That decision is a modelling choice, and it belongs in the analysis plan.

title: From the question to the model
text:
The grid, drawn



Ten chambered enclosures, five warming steps at ambient CO2 and the same five at elevated CO2, plus two unchambered ambient plots.


Each circle is one enclosure, and it receives one warming step and one CO₂ atmosphere. The two open squares were never assigned a warming level.

Count to ten circles, then point at the two open squares. Those two cannot sit on a warming slope until the analysis plan says what their warming value is. Do not invent plot numbers: the sketch is the grid, not a map of which plot is which step.

title: From the question to the model
text:
What is measured here
The response in this dataset is a gene copy number per gram of dry peat, from quantitative PCR (Roth et al. 2024).

12 plots \(\times\) 9 depth increments \(\times\) 2 sampling months in 2021: 216 rows
Bacterial, archaeal, and fungal copies, each with a log column
Missing numeric values are coded \(-9999\) in the published file

A qPCR copy number is an estimated abundance, not a counted integer. It is a positive, strongly skewed continuous response, so it belongs with the transformation discussion and not with the Poisson.

Be explicit that this is not a count, even though it looks like one. Treating a qPCR abundance as Poisson would be a category error, and it is a mistake the room will have seen. The sentinel value is the other teaching point: 15 values in this file are -9999, and a script that reads the column as a number without that rule will report a mean of about -9999 times the missing fraction. The rule lives in prepare-teaching-data.R and nowhere else.

title: From the question to the model
section: The sentinel is a documented rule
text:
The sentinel is a documented rule

# "Missing numeric data are indicated by -9999" (dataset documentation)
numeric_cols <- c("Bacteria_copy_dry", "Archaea_copy_dry", "Fungal_copy_dry")
for (nm in numeric_cols) {
  spruce_raw[[nm]][spruce_raw[[nm]] == -9999] <- NA_real_
}

Fifteen values across the nine numeric columns are sentinels. One of the 216 bacterial measurements is missing.

Short slide. The message is that the rule came from the dataset documentation, not from a guess, and that it is written once in a script rather than repeated in every analysis. Link it forward to the missing-data pitfall: this is missingness you can describe, which is the easy case.

title: From the question to the model
text:
The scale of the response



Left, raw bacterial copies against depth: a few surface values dominate. Right, the same data on a log10 scale with a fitted straight line.


On the log scale the fall with depth is about \(-0.079\) in \(\log_{10}\) copies per 10 cm, and depth alone accounts for \(R^2 = 0.23\).

The left panel is why the dataset ships a log column. The right panel is the transformation argument in its legitimate form: the transform is chosen because the mechanism is multiplicative, not because a normality test failed. Flag that this slope is a description of 12 plots at one site in one year, not a global law, and that the interval for it needs the plot structure on the next slide.
Going further. If \(\log Y\) is normal with mean \(m\) and variance \(\sigma^2\), then \(\mathbb{E}(Y) = \exp(m + \sigma^2/2)\), so back-transforming a fitted mean on the log scale gives the median, not the mean. Duan’s smearing estimator (📄 Smearing estimate: a nonparametric retransformation method, Journal of the American Statistical Association, 1983) corrects this without assuming normality. A Gamma or log-normal GLM with a log link targets \(\log \mathbb{E}(Y \mid \mathbf{x})\) directly. \(R^2\) depends on the range of depth sampled, so it is a property of this design, not of the process.

title: From the question to the model
text:
One line per plot



Depth profiles of log10 bacterial copies, one line per plot, split by sampling month.


Nine depths inside one plot are not nine independent plots. Where the replicate is depends on the question: where the replicate is.

This figure is the hierarchy made visible. Each line is a plot; the points on it are depths. A regression on 215 rows that ignores the plot has about 12 units of real information about warming, not 215. That is the same arithmetic as the CA-SYS subplots. Both datasets make the same point, which is why the design block can treat them together.
Going further. With \(m\) rows per plot and intraclass correlation \(\rho\), the effective sample size for a plot-level contrast is \(n/\{1 + (m - 1)\rho\}\). Here \(m\) is about 18 (nine depths by two months), so even a modest \(\rho = 0.3\) cuts 215 rows to about 35, and as \(\rho \to 1\) it tends to the 12 plots. For a covariate that varies within plots, such as depth, the plot effect instead removes between-plot noise and can increase precision.

title: From the question to the model
section: The model the design is asking for
text:
The model the design is asking for
For plot \(j\), depth \(i\):






Model


\[
\log_{10} Y_{ij} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \mathrm{depth}_{ij} + \beta_2 x_{1j} + \beta_3 x_{2j} + \beta_4 x_{1j} x_{2j} + u_j + \varepsilon_{ij}
\]




\(x_{1j}\): warming assigned to the enclosure
\(x_{2j}\): elevated \(\mathrm{CO}_2\) against ambient
\(u_j\): plot-level departure, \(u_j \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_u^2)\)

A \(t\)-test of “warm against cool” is a different estimand, and a poorer one.

Point at the indices: j is the plot, i is the depth increment. The interaction is the scientific question the design was built for, which is why binning the five warming levels into two groups throws the design away. Two minutes, then move on: the fitting details are in the design block.
Going further. \(\sigma_u^2\) is usually estimated by restricted maximum likelihood (Patterson and Thompson, 1971), which maximises the likelihood of error contrasts and removes the downward bias of the ML variance estimate, analogous to dividing by \(n - p\). Because \(x_{1j}\) and \(x_{2j}\) vary only between plots, their standard errors are driven by about 12 plots minus the plot-level parameters, so small-sample corrections to the denominator degrees of freedom (Satterthwaite, Kenward–Roger) matter. The regression design across five warming levels uses the gradient to estimate a slope, which is more powerful than an ANOVA on binned levels when the response is close to linear (Cottingham et al., 2005).

All four rows are exponential-dispersion families, \(f(y) = \exp[\{y\theta - b(\theta)\}/\phi + c(y, \phi)]\), with \(\mu = b'(\theta)\) and \(\mathrm{Var}(Y) = \phi\, b''(\theta) = \phi V(\mu)\). Choosing a family is choosing \(V(\mu)\); the link is a separate choice, and the canonical one is \(g = (b')^{-1}\). That shared form is why one fitting algorithm, iteratively reweighted least squares, and one deviance-based toolkit serve every row. See Agresti (Agresti 2015).

Six purposes, six different \(\mu\)

A significant coefficient does not say which of these you did. The three we will separate are explain, predict, and confirm.






Riley and colleagues ask authors to say whether the work is descriptive or causal, prognostic or predictive, exploratory or confirmatory. One minute.

title: From the question to the model
section: 1 · PICO, when the question is a comparison
text:
1 · PICO, when the question is a comparison



PICO diagram: Patient or population, Intervention or exposure, Comparison, and Outcome, each with a prompt.


For a designed contrast or a systematic comparison, name population, intervention or exposure, comparison, and outcome (Riley et al. 2022).

Walk through one row of the figure aloud: population is not “the dataset”, it is the system and the unit that carries the contrast. Do not linger; the exercise slide is next.

title: From the question to the model
text:
1 · Start with the question







Question
Target




Causal
What would change in \(Y\) if the exposure \(x\) changed


Prediction
How close \(\hat{\mu}\) is to \(Y\) for a new unit


Exploratory
Hypotheses to test later; the fit is not the final claim


Confirmatory
A contrast and covariates fixed before the data



Write down which row you are answering. The comparison form is PICO.

Point at the first two rows. Ask the room which branch their PICO belongs to. Many carbon papers mix explanation and prediction in one sentence; naming the branch is the fix. Ninety seconds.

title: From the question to the model
text:
1 · Explain, predict, or confirm

Explain. Which covariates, and how large is \(\beta\)? The coefficient and its interval are the result.
Predict. How close is \(\hat{Y}\) on a unit the fit did not see? The score is a prediction error, not a \(p\)-value.
Confirm. The contrast, the covariates, and the claim were written down before the fit. A search until something is significant is exploratory.

MetricGate (April 2025) works the first two through a linear model and a random forest. Confirmatory is the pre-specification on the six purposes. The checks for a prediction are three different questions.

Step the fragments slowly. The common mistake is to treat a small \(p\) on \(\hat\beta_j\) as proof of good prediction. Ask which metric they would put in the abstract for each purpose. Two minutes.
Going further. Shmueli’s article “To explain or to predict?” (Statistical Science, 2010) is the standard reference. The expected squared prediction error at a new \(\mathbf{x}\) decomposes as \(\sigma^2 + \mathrm{bias}^2\{\hat\mu(\mathbf{x})\} + \mathrm{Var}\{\hat\mu(\mathbf{x})\}\), so a deliberately biased but less variable model (dropped covariates, shrinkage) can predict better than the correctly specified one. Explanation instead needs \(\hat\beta_j\) to be consistent for a named causal or structural quantity, which is a statement about bias, not about total error. Confirmatory inference adds a third requirement: the error rate of the test is only valid if the hypothesis, the covariates and the analysis were fixed before the data, otherwise the selection step must be accounted for (post-selection inference, Berk and colleagues, Annals of Statistics, 2013).

title: From the question to the model
section: 1 · A hold-out score does not certify the coefficient
text:
1 · A hold-out score does not certify the coefficient



A hold-out score answers how close \(\hat{Y}\) is on new rows
It does not say that \(\hat\beta\) is unbiased
It does not say the path from \(x\) to \(Y\) is the one you would intervene on

When the claim is about \(\beta\):

Check the linear assumptions
Refit after removing influential rows

Keep the hold-out for a prediction. Ranking, calibration, and the decision are three further checks.




Cross-validation is not a substitute for a causal estimand or for checking influence on \(\hat\beta\). If the room is quiet, ask: “Your AUC is 0.9 — can you still intervene on \(x_j\)?” That usually opens the right debate.
Going further. \(K\)-fold cross-validation estimates the expected prediction error of the fitting procedure, averaged over training sets, rather than the error of the one fitted model; Bates, Hastie and Tibshirani (Journal of the American Statistical Association, 2024) show that the naive interval around a cross-validation score under-covers for that reason. Rows are only exchangeable if they are independent: with clustered data a random split leaks the cluster into both folds and the score is optimistic, so the folds must hold out whole clusters \(j\). A low prediction error is compatible with a biased \(\hat\beta\), because a proxy or a collider can carry the predictive signal. Influence on \(\hat\beta\) is checked with Cook’s distance or DFBETAS, not with a hold-out score.

title: From the question to the model
section: 2 · An effect, an interval, and a reason it matters
text:
2 · An effect, an interval, and a reason it matters



Two published risk ratios. A narrow interval sits just below 1. A wide interval runs from 0.40 to 1.10 and crosses 1.


The two intervals are the published example in Riley and colleagues (Riley et al. 2022).

Two intervals, two different failures. The narrow one is precise and small: detected, and possibly irrelevant. The wide one is large and uncertain: absence of evidence, not evidence of absence. The CA-SYS rate ratio later today is the first kind, and the tillage richness contrast is the second. Neither is read off a p-value.
Going further. A \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) confidence interval is the set of null values \(\theta_0\) that a level-\(\alpha\) test would not reject, so it carries strictly more information than one \(p\) against \(\theta_0 = 0\) (test–interval duality, Hogg, McKean and Craig, Introduction to Mathematical Statistics (Hogg et al. 2019)). For a ratio such as a risk ratio the interval is built on the log scale, \(\log\widehat{\mathrm{RR}} \pm 1.96\,\mathrm{SE}\), and exponentiated, which is why the two intervals on the figure are asymmetric. The coverage is a property of the procedure over replicates; a given interval either contains the true value or it does not.

title: From the question to the model
text:
2 · Detection is not importance





Infographic contrasting a statistically detectable effect with an effect that also exceeds a minimal clinically important difference.




Statistical evidence: could the data have come from a world with no effect?
Practical evidence: a minimal important difference, set before the fit. It is not a formula, and \(p\) does not supply it (Olszewski)
Replace the clinical threshold with a flux, a stock, or a decision that would change
Keep the estimate and the interval in the sentence (Halsey et al. 2015)



This slide used to be two, which said the same thing twice. The one idea is that significance and importance are separate judgements and only one of them comes from the data. Ask the room what change in soil carbon would alter a management decision. Most groups have never written that number down, which is the point. In a confirmatory analysis it is written before the fit.

title: From the question to the model
section: 2 · A yes-or-no decision has two errors
text:
2 · A yes-or-no decision has two errors



Two-by-two table of a hypothesis test: Type I error when a true null is rejected, Type II error when a false null is not rejected.


A Type I error rejects the null when it is true; its long-run rate, when the test is calibrated, is \(\alpha\). A Type II error fails to reject the null when it is false; its rate is \(\beta\), and the power is \(1 - \beta\) (Biswas).

The table is a decision table, and it only makes sense once you have agreed to make a yes-or-no decision. That is a choice, not an obligation. The two rates are properties of the procedure across many replicates, not statements about the study in front of you. Keep that distinction, because the next slide needs it.
Going further. This is the Neyman–Pearson framework: fix \(\alpha\), then choose the rejection region that maximises power \(1 - \beta(\theta)\) at each alternative. The Neyman–Pearson lemma gives the most powerful test of a simple null against a simple alternative, the likelihood-ratio test; uniformly most powerful tests exist only in special cases, such as one-sided tests in a one-parameter exponential family. Power depends on the true effect, the noise and the sample size: for a two-sample \(z\) test with \(n\) per arm and standard deviation \(\sigma\), \(1-\beta \approx \Phi\left(|\delta|\sqrt{n/2}/\sigma - z_{1-\alpha/2}\right)\). The Type I and Type II rates are not the error rates of the claims made; that needs the prior share of true nulls, as on the \(\alpha\) slide.

title: From the question to the model
text:
2 · \(p\) is not that rate
If the treatment has no effect, a \(p\) of 0.03 means that 3% of replicate studies would obtain an effect this large or larger.

Comparing that number with \(\alpha\) is the yes-or-no decision
The number itself is a probability about the data, not about the hypothesis
\(\alpha\) is fixed before the data; \(p\) is computed from them

The careful statement is the replicate definition, and the rate of false assertions is \(\alpha\).

The commonest error in the room will be to read p as the probability that the null is true. Say the two conditional probabilities out loud: P(data this extreme given no effect) against P(no effect given the data). Only the first is available from a frequentist test, and only the second is what most readers want.
Going further. For a continuous test statistic \(T\) with null distribution \(F_0\), \(p = 1 - F_0(T_{\mathrm{obs}})\) is itself a random variable, and under the null it is exactly uniform on \((0, 1)\) (probability integral transform). Rejecting when \(p \le \alpha\) therefore has size \(\alpha\), which is the only sense in which \(p\) and \(\alpha\) meet. Under an alternative, \(p\) is stochastically smaller, but its distribution is wide unless power is high. Bayes’ theorem gives \(P(H_0 \mid \text{data}) = P(\text{data} \mid H_0) P(H_0) / P(\text{data})\): turning \(p\) into a posterior requires a prior and a likelihood under the alternative, which a test does not supply.

title: From the question to the model
section: 2 · A p-value is about the data
text:
2 · A p-value is about the data
Under identical replicates of this experiment, with the effect set to zero, \(p\) is the probability of a result more extreme than the one in hand (Harrell, ch. 22).
A \(p\) of 0.06 says that, under the model and the null, a replicate would be more extreme about 6 times in 100. It does not say that the null has probability 0.06.






Write “given \(H_0\)” on the board if you have one. The 0.06 example is deliberately awkward — neither side of 0.05 — to keep the focus on the conditional, not on the threshold ritual.
Going further. Formally \(p = P_{H_0}(T \ge t_{\mathrm{obs}})\), a tail area computed under every assumption of the model, not only the zero effect: independence, the error distribution, the sampling plan and the choice of \(T\). “More extreme” needs an ordering of possible results, so a one-sided and a two-sided test give different \(p\) for the same data. With a discrete statistic (counts, ranks) \(p\) is not exactly uniform under the null and the test is conservative; mid-\(p\) values correct part of this. Harrell’s Biostatistics for Biomedical Research, chapter on hypothesis testing, and the ASA statement (Wasserstein and Lazar, The American Statistician, 2016) are the standard references.

title: From the question to the model
section: 2 · α is a rate of false assertions
text:
2 · α is a rate of false assertions
\(\alpha\) is the long-run probability of asserting an effect when the effect is exactly zero. It is not the probability that a positive result is false, and it is not “the probability of an error”.
A procedure that assumes the null cannot report the probability that the null is true. Fisher’s 1956 wording treated a 1% test as a 1% rate of mistaken decisions, which swaps \(P(\text{assert} \mid H_0)\) with \(P(H_0 \mid \text{assert})\) (Harrell).

\(\alpha\) is chosen before data; \(p\) is computed after. The Fisher quote is the Bayesian confusion in one line — read it slowly.
Going further. The probability that a positive result is false is the false discovery proportion among assertions. With a prior share \(\pi_0\) of true nulls, \(P(H_0 \mid \text{assert}) = \alpha\pi_0 / \{\alpha\pi_0 + (1-\beta)(1-\pi_0)\}\). With \(\alpha = 0.05\), power \(0.8\) and \(\pi_0 = 0.9\), that is \(0.045 / (0.045 + 0.08) \approx 0.36\), far above \(5\%\); Ioannidis (“Why most published research findings are false”, PLoS Medicine, 2005) and Colquhoun (Royal Society Open Science, 2014) work this arithmetic. It is the same quantity that the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure controls in expectation over many tests (Farcomeni 2008).

title: From the question to the model
section: 2 · The tail belongs to a model
text:
2 · The tail belongs to a model
Guillaume Rousselet takes a one-sample, one-sided \(t\) test: \(n = 50\), \(t = 1.52\), \(p = 0.0670\) when the imaginary experiments are normal, independent, of fixed size, and always analysed with that \(t\) test.
Sampling the same tail from the beta distribution the scores actually follow moves the simulated \(p\) from 0.0675 to 0.0804. Change the model and the number moves (garstats 2026).






This is the “same \(t\), different likelihood” slide. You are not asking them to abandon \(t\) tests; you are showing that \(p\) is computed under a story. If they only remember one line: the tail belongs to the model.
Going further. The \(t\) test is exact only when the observations are independent and Gaussian; otherwise its level relies on the central limit theorem, and the error in the tail probability is of order \(n^{-1/2}\) for skewed data (an Edgeworth expansion). Far tails converge slowest, so small \(p\) values are the least trustworthy. A parametric bootstrap or a permutation test computes the tail under a different, sometimes weaker, model; a permutation test is exact under exchangeability of the units under the null. Bounded scores, such as those in Rousselet’s example, are not Gaussian at any \(n\), which is why the simulated tail moved.

title: From the question to the model
section: 2 · The same p, a shrinking effect
text:
2 · The same p, a shrinking effect
Lantz keeps \(p = 0.0253\) while a preference for treatment X shrinks toward a coin toss. These are the two ends of his table.



\(n\)
Prefer X

\(< 0.01\)



The first would change a choice. The second would not. The interval is what a large sample tightens, which is why the large sample is still the better experiment. Put the estimate next to a pre-stated consequence. The opposite failure is a small study that still declares an effect: the size and the sign.

Same \(p\), opposite practical meaning. Ask what proportion “prefer X” would need to change a management rule in their project. The table is Lantz’s arithmetic, not your data.
Going further. A consistent test has power tending to 1 against any fixed alternative, so with enough data every non-zero effect, however trivial, gives a small \(p\); the standardised statistic grows like \(\sqrt{n}\,\delta/\sigma\). Holding \(p\) fixed as \(n\) grows therefore forces the effect to shrink like \(n^{-1/2}\), which is Lantz’s table. Lindley’s paradox is the Bayesian counterpart: at fixed \(p\) and growing \(n\), the Bayes factor increasingly favours the point null. Cohen’s \(h = 2\arcsin\sqrt{\pi_1} - 2\arcsin\sqrt{\pi_2}\) is the variance-stabilised difference of proportions.

title: From the question to the model
section: 2 · A small study can detect the wrong size
text:
2 · A small study can detect the wrong size



Ten thousand simulated mean differences. Significant results lie far above the true difference of 1, or below zero with the sign reversed.


Gelman and Carlin: Type M is how many times too large a significant estimate is. Type S is how often that significant estimate has the wrong sign.

Type M and Type S only apply when someone filters on “significant”. The scatter is the visual; the definitions are the labels. Link to low power in the next slide.
Going further. With an estimate \(\hat\theta \sim N(\theta, s^2)\), the Type S rate is \(P(\hat\theta < -z s) / \{P(\hat\theta > z s) + P(\hat\theta < -z s)\}\) for \(\theta > 0\), and the exaggeration ratio is \(\mathbb{E}(|\hat\theta| \mid |\hat\theta| > z s)/\theta\), both functions of \(\theta/s\) only. Gelman and Carlin’s retrodesign calculation evaluates them at a plausible effect size taken from outside the study, not at the observed estimate, which would be circular. This is the winner’s curse: selecting on significance is a truncation, and the truncated mean is biased away from zero.

title: From the question to the model
text:
3 · Three mechanisms



Three cards: MCAR as entirely random, MAR as influenced by an observed variable, MNAR as influenced by an unobserved variable.


Figure credit on the source image: @daansan_ml.

Name the three letters only after the room has tried. MCAR is the idealisation; MNAR is where honest papers stop pretending listwise deletion is neutral.
Going further. Rubin (Biometrika, 1976) defines the mechanisms through the distribution of the missingness indicator \(R\) given the full data: MCAR when \(P(R \mid Y_{\mathrm{obs}}, Y_{\mathrm{mis}}) = P(R)\), MAR when it depends only on \(Y_{\mathrm{obs}}\), and MNAR otherwise. Under MAR, and if the parameters of the missingness model are distinct from those of the data model, the mechanism is ignorable for likelihood and Bayesian inference: the observed-data likelihood alone gives valid estimates. Complete-case analysis is unbiased under MCAR, and for a regression also when missingness depends only on the covariates \(\mathbf{x}\), not on \(Y\). MAR cannot be tested against MNAR from the observed data alone, which is why MNAR calls for a sensitivity analysis (Little and Rubin, Statistical Analysis with Missing Data).

title: From the question to the model
section: 3 · Missing data are part of the design
text:
3 · Missing data are part of the design







Avoid
Prefer




Zero or mean fill
Report extent of missingness in \(Y\) and in \(x\)


Indiscriminate complete-case deletion
Name the mechanism you assume; multiple imputation when MAR is defensible



Report how much is missing, in \(Y\) and in \(x\), and what you did. Zero-fill, a mean fill, and dropping every incomplete row are assumptions, not defaults (Riley et al. 2022). Definitions: three mechanisms.

This is the answer to the opening question. Ask which row someone has used as a default. Complete case is fine only when you can defend MCAR or a clear MAR story.
Going further. Multiple imputation draws \(M\) completed datasets from the posterior predictive distribution of the missing values, fits the analysis model to each, and pools with Rubin’s rules: the estimate is the mean \(\bar\theta\) and the variance is \(\bar W + (1 + 1/M)B\), with \(\bar W\) the mean within-imputation variance and \(B\) the between-imputation variance. The imputation model must contain the outcome \(Y\) and every variable of the analysis model, including interactions and non-linear terms, otherwise the associations are biased towards zero. Mean imputation underestimates the variance and attenuates correlations; a single imputation, however good, ignores \(B\). Van Buuren’s Flexible Imputation of Missing Data is the practical reference for chained equations (mice).

title: From the question to the model
text:
4 · Do not dichotomise a continuous \(x\)





flowchart LR
  cut["cut at 130"]
  v129["129 → low"]
  v131["131 → high"]
  v220["220 → high"]
  cut --- v129
  cut --- v131
  cut --- v220













Cost of a cut
Better




Loses order; unstable threshold
Keep \(x\) continuous: \(Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \epsilon\)



A threshold throws away order, spends power, and makes the result depend on the cut (Riley et al. 2022). Altman and Royston (2006) is the short note.

The absurd pairing is the teaching point: 131 with 220, not with 129. Ask if anyone has binned soil moisture at a round number because the software defaulted to tertiles.
Going further. For a normal \(x\) split at its median, the correlation with the dichotomised variable is \(\sqrt{2/\pi} \approx 0.80\) of the original, so the efficiency is \(2/\pi \approx 0.64\): about a third of the sample is thrown away (Cohen, Applied Psychological Measurement, 1983). Splits away from the median lose more. The step function also misspecifies \(\mathbb{E}(Y \mid x)\) within each group, which leaves residual confounding when \(x\) is a confounder. Royston, Altman and Sauerbrei (Statistics in Medicine, 2006) give the full case.

title: From the question to the model
section: 7 · \(I^2\) is not the size of the heterogeneity
text:
7 · \(I^2\) is not the size of the heterogeneity







Quantity
Read as




\(\tau^2\)
Absolute spread of true site effects


\(I^2\)
Share of scatter that is heterogeneity relative to sampling noise


Study-level regression on proportions
Not the same as a within-site slope (ecological bias)



\(I^2\) is a relative share of variance. Small studies can show a small \(I^2\) while the between-site variance is large. Report that variance. A regression on site means is not the core-level slope. The arithmetic starts at one site, one estimate. Sampling noise shrinks with \(n\); a bias does not (random and systematic error).

This slide is the warning label; the next ten minutes are the arithmetic. If someone quotes \(I^2 = 25\%\) as “low heterogeneity”, ask for \(\tau^2\) in the effect’s units.
Going further. Higgins and Thompson (Statistics in Medicine, 2002) introduced \(I^2\) as the proportion of total variation due to heterogeneity rather than chance; it depends on the precision of the studies and therefore on their size, while \(\tau^2\) does not. Rücker and colleagues (BMC Medical Research Methodology, 2008) show that \(I^2\) tends to 100% as the study sizes grow, for any fixed \(\tau^2 > 0\). Ecological bias, or aggregation bias, arises because a regression across site means estimates the between-site association, which mixes the within-site slope with between-site confounding (Greenland and Morgenstern, International Journal of Epidemiology, 1989).

title: From the question to the model
text:
7 · One site, one estimate
In this block \(i\) is a study or a site, and \(y_i\) is that site’s estimated effect. It is not the core-level response \(Y\).
\[
y_i = \theta_i + \varepsilon_i, \qquad \varepsilon_i \sim N(0, s_i^2)
\]

\(y_i\): the estimate you observe
\(\theta_i\): the true effect at that site
\(s_i^2\): the sampling variance of the estimate

Two sites with the same \(\theta\) can still disagree, because of \(\varepsilon_i\).

Say the change of index once. Here i is the site, which is the cluster. The core-level response is still Y, and it is not on this slide. About one minute. The next two slides separate that sampling noise from a bias that more rows will not remove.
Going further. In a meta-analysis \(s_i^2\) is treated as known, although it is itself estimated; this is harmless when the within-site samples are large but biases small-study meta-analyses, especially for log odds ratios with few events. The normal approximation \(y_i \sim N(\theta_i, s_i^2)\) rests on the asymptotic normality of the site estimator, for example a maximum-likelihood estimator with variance from the inverse Fisher information. Borenstein and colleagues’ Introduction to Meta-Analysis is the readable reference for the whole block.

title: From the question to the model
text:
7 · Random error shrinks
Thiese, Ronna, and Ott define random error as noise around the true value, above and below it. It is not a bias. On the previous slide it is \(\varepsilon_i\), with variance \(s_i^2\). A larger sample at that site makes \(s_i\) smaller, which is the same move as the standard error.
Selection, a misread instrument, and a confounder are not this noise. They shift every row the same way.

Connect \(\varepsilon_i\) to the standard error they already know. Random error is what replication within a site would average down; confounding is not that.

\[\theta_i = \mu + u_i, \quad u_i \sim N(0, \tau^2)\]

Green is observed. Red is latent. A rectangle is fixed. The plate is the index \(i\). The same two lines are a hierarchical model: fixed and random name the target.

Left plate: \(\theta_i\) is fixed at \(\mu\), and only \(y_i\) is random. Right plate: \(\theta_i\) is red because it is not seen. Do not say the random-effects mean is automatically the causal effect. One minute on each column.

title: From the question to the model
text:
8 · A prediction needs three checks








Check
Question
Sketch on next slides




Discrimination
Do high \(\hat\pi\) rank above low?
AUC


Calibration
In bins, does \(\bar Y \approx \hat\pi\)?
Calibration plot


Utility
Does the score beat treat-all / treat-none at some \(t\)?
Net benefit



Discrimination, calibration, and usefulness at a decision threshold are different questions (Riley et al. 2022). A large AUC with a miscalibrated probability still misleads the decision.
We will not fit a prediction model today. The three sketches that follow are drawings, not fitted scores. They belong to the prediction purpose, not to an explanation of \(\beta\).

Say explicitly that you will not teach ROC construction today. The table is the map; the drawings are teaching arithmetic. Two minutes for this slide, then one minute per dimension.
Going further. Steyerberg’s Clinical Prediction Models and the TRIPOD guidance organise validation in this order. Discrimination is invariant to any monotone transformation of \(\hat\pi\), so it cannot detect a miscalibrated model; calibration and net benefit are not. The Brier score \(n^{-1}\sum_i (Y_i - \hat\pi_i)^2\) is a proper scoring rule that mixes both, and decomposes into calibration (reliability) and refinement terms. All three must be estimated on data the model did not see, or corrected for optimism by the bootstrap (Harrell, Regression Modeling Strategies).

title: From the question to the model
text:
8 · Discrimination is the ranking
\[\mathrm{AUC} = \Pr(\hat\pi_{\mathrm{event}} > \hat\pi_{\mathrm{none}})\]
Teaching arithmetic, not a fitted model: 8 of 10 pairs ordered correctly is an AUC of 0.8. The diagonal is 0.5.



Two ROC sketches. The red curve lies on the diagonal. The green curve rises toward the top-left corner.



The 8-of-10 pairs line is the only number to remember. Red is chance ranking; green is usable separation. Do not conflate with calibration.
Going further. The AUC equals the Mann–Whitney statistic \(U/(n_1 n_0)\), the proportion of event–non-event pairs ranked correctly, with ties counted one half (Hanley and McNeil, Radiology, 1982). It is the area under the ROC curve of sensitivity against \(1 -\) specificity over all thresholds, so it averages over thresholds nobody would use. It depends on the case mix: a more heterogeneous population gives a higher AUC for the same model. For a survival outcome the analogue is Harrell’s \(C\) index.

title: From the question to the model
text:
9 · Repeated rows are not replicates





flowchart TD
  j["cluster j (enclosure, site, patient)"]
  j --> i1["observation i"]
  j --> i2["observation i"]
  j --> i3["observation i"]






\[Y_{ij} = \beta_0 + u_j + \beta^\top \mathbf{x}_{ij} + \epsilon_{ij}, \qquad u_j \sim N(0,\sigma_u^2), \qquad \rho = \frac{\sigma_u^2}{\sigma_u^2 + \sigma^2}\]
Ignoring the cluster pretends that rows in the same enclosure are as different as rows in different enclosures (Riley et al. 2022). The model is a random intercept.

Index \(j\) is the unit that received the treatment; \(i\) is the repeated measure or sub-sample. Ask them to name both indices for their dataset before you show the row count slide.
Going further. In the random-intercept model the intraclass correlation \(\rho\) is the correlation between two observations in the same cluster. For a cluster-level treatment with \(m\) observations per cluster, the variance of the treatment effect is inflated by the design effect \(1 + (m-1)\rho\) (Kish, Survey Sampling), so the effective sample size is \(nm/\{1 + (m-1)\rho\}\): even \(\rho = 0.1\) with \(m = 20\) nearly triples the variance. Ignoring the cluster gives standard errors that are too small for cluster-level covariates. The variance components are estimated by REML, which corrects the downward bias of maximum likelihood for \(\sigma_u^2\) by accounting for the fixed effects (Patterson and Thompson, Biometrika, 1971).

title: From the question to the model
text:
10 · Three arrows, three estimands





flowchart LR
  moisture[Soil moisture]
  carbon[Organic carbon]
  taxon[Taxon count Y]
  moisture --> carbon
  moisture --> taxon
  carbon --> taxon






If the question is the effect of carbon on the taxon, moisture is a confounder: it feeds both. Adjusting for a mediator, or for a collider, answers a different question. The same diagram, as a causal claim, is a confounder in the soil table.

Trace the three arrows with your cursor. The estimand question is: do you want total, direct, or predictive association? Ninety seconds.
Going further. In this graph moisture opens the back-door path carbon \(\leftarrow\) moisture \(\rightarrow Y\), so \(\{\text{moisture}\}\) is a sufficient adjustment set for the total effect of carbon. The set is read off the graph by d-separation, not from the data: the same joint distribution is compatible with several graphs, and the data can only rule out graphs whose implied conditional independences fail. Conditioning on a collider, a common effect of exposure and outcome, induces an association between its causes (Berkson’s bias); conditioning on a mediator removes the indirect part of a total effect. The free tool DAGitty (Textor and colleagues) lists the adjustment sets and the testable implications of a drawn graph.

title: From the question to the model
section: 11 · Show that the conclusion can move
text:
11 · Show that the conclusion can move





flowchart TD
  main["Main analysis: estimate and interval"]
  main --> miss["Missing-data assumption"]
  main --> time["Time-to-event shape"]
  main --> model["Model / link / distribution"]
  main --> prior["Prior or penalty choice"]
  miss --> stab["Does the conclusion move?"]
  time --> stab
  model --> stab
  prior --> stab






A constant hazard ratio, a “vague” prior, or a complete-case fit can each carry the result. Refit under a second defensible assumption and say what moved (Riley et al. 2022). For an observational claim, sensitivity is the report.

Sensitivity is not “try everything until it sticks”. Name one alternative assumption per panel and report direction and size of change. Observational work gets the causal link at the end of the sentence.
Going further. For missing data, a delta-adjusted pattern-mixture analysis shifts the imputed values of the missing \(Y\) by \(\delta\) and reports the tipping point \(\delta\) at which the conclusion changes; \(\delta = 0\) is MAR. For unmeasured confounding, the E-value of VanderWeele and Ding (Annals of Internal Medicine, 2017), \(\mathrm{RR} + \sqrt{\mathrm{RR}(\mathrm{RR}-1)}\), is the minimum strength of association, on the risk-ratio scale, that a confounder would need with both exposure and outcome to explain the estimate away. For a prior, the analysis is repeated under a sceptical and an enthusiastic prior. A sensitivity analysis should vary an assumption the data cannot check; refitting under assumptions that the data already reject is model checking, not sensitivity.

SAMPL, on the EQUATOR Network, is the checklist we will use at the end Lang and Altman, 2015. The four lines for this room are SAMPL, in workshop language.

SAMPL is the one they will see again in the reproducibility block. Pick one “avoid” row and ask for a rewrite from the room. One minute.

title: From the question to the model
text:
Where we go deeper
Of these twelve, the next hour stays with a problem the poster assumes you have already solved: the distribution of \(Y\).
Soil counts, fluxes, and compositions are often skewed, bounded, discrete, or full of zeros. A Gaussian linear model is then the wrong likelihood, even when the question, the estimand, and the design are clear. Next: the shape of \(Y\).

Close the pitfalls hour on purpose: clear question does not imply Gaussian \(Y\). Thirty seconds, then advance to section 3.

title: From the question to the model
section: The pipeline rewrites the column first
text:
The pipeline rewrites the column first



A machine-learning pipeline from data collection through feature transformation, selection, dimension reduction, and modelling, with model evaluation and tuning circled.


Hartmann and Rudolph, EGU 2026 short course SC2.28, draw the usual order. The circled step is where the score is judged. A rewrite of the column that changes the mean shows up there as a number you cannot interpret. This hour is about that rewrite.

Trace the pipeline left to right and linger on the circled evaluation box. Ask what happens if a log or library-size normalisation is applied before the model is chosen—the metric still looks fine while the estimand changed. This slide sets the stake for everything that follows about transforms versus links.

title: From the question to the model
section: The shape is often the scientific object
text:
The shape is often the scientific object
Environmental \(Y\) is often:

skewed, and strictly positive
a count, or a composition
full of zeros, or censored at a detection limit
dependent in time or in space

A Gaussian lm can still be a useful approximation for a mean. It is a poor default when the support of \(Y\) makes the approximation impossible. This hour follows where we go deeper. Skew, in particular, is ordinary: Quetilismus.

Read the bullet list as a checklist against CA-SYS and SPRUCE: counts, zeros, composition, dependence. The closing sentence is deliberately soft—a Gaussian mean can be fine—before the support argument bites. Link forward to Quetilismus as the cultural habit behind ignoring skew.

title: From the question to the model
text:
Quetilismus
🔗 Adrian Olszewski names the habit after Edgeworth’s word for Quetelet. A unimodal curve is treated as a normal curve. Skew is then a defect to repair: drop the tails, wait for a larger sample, or transform until the histogram looks symmetric.

Name Quetilismus once, then list the three repairs: trim tails, wait for \(n\), transform until symmetric. Students often recognise their own lab practice in the third.

title: From the question to the model
text:
Skew is a description
A skewed description of a real process does not become less legitimate because the sample grew. Treating the normal law as the dominant description sets aside the mechanisms that generate the skew.
The next slide is the modelling consequence. The Gaussian assumption, when it is used, is about \(Y \mid \mathbf{x}\), not about the raw histogram.

Quote the Medium opening idea: skew is not illegitimate because \(n\) grew. Bridge to the next slide with the conditional phrase \(Y \mid \mathbf{x}\). A common misread is to treat marginal skew as proof the linear model failed before any covariates are in the model.

title: From the question to the model
text:
How to read the plot 🔍



Two QQ plots. Left: residuals from a Gaussian response sit near the reference line. Right: residuals from a Gaussian linear model fitted to Poisson counts bend up in the right tail.



Pair with the previous code slide: left panel is the sanity check, right panel is the misspecified count. Finger the right-tail lift as variance growing with the mean, not “non-normality” in the abstract. The preceding slide showed how those panels were produced.

title: From the question to the model
section: Four shapes on the QQ plot
text:
Four shapes on the QQ plot



Four normal QQ plots: Gaussian points on the line, heavy tails as an S-curve, right skew as a concave-up bend, light tails as a flat S.


Ends that flare are heavy tails. A concave-up bend is right skew. A concave-down bend is left skew. A flat S is light tails. The shaded ribbon on the Gaussian panel is a generic band. The band to use is the tail-sensitive one.

Point at each panel in the four-shape figure while naming flare, concave-up, concave-down, flat S. The generic ribbon on the Gaussian panel is not the tail-sensitive band—preview the bandType = "ts" slide. Students confuse heavy tails with right skew; keep the vocabulary separate.

title: From the question to the model
text:
A tail-sensitive band
The ribbon to draw is the simultaneous tail-sensitive band of Aldor-Noiman and colleagues (2013). In qqplotr that is bandType = "ts". It is implemented for a normal QQ plot. A pointwise ribbon is a different object.

ggplot(residuals, aes(sample = residual)) +
  qqplotr::stat_qq_band(bandType = "ts") +
  qqplotr::stat_qq_line() +
  qqplotr::stat_qq_point()

Points outside that band are the departure. A \(p\)-value from a normality test is not a summary of the same picture. The workshop residuals are the two QQ plots above, read this way.

Highlight bandType = "ts" in the code chunk—normal QQ only. Contrast simultaneous tail-sensitive band with a pointwise ribbon. Tie back to the generated Gaussian-versus-count residuals once students see points outside the band.
Going further. A pointwise 95% band covers each quantile with probability 0.95, so with \(n\) points the chance that at least one falls outside is far above 5%. A simultaneous band is calibrated so that the whole curve lies inside with probability 0.95. Aldor-Noiman and colleagues (The American Statistician, 2013) build it from the \(\mathrm{Beta}(i, n + 1 - i)\) law of uniform order statistics, which keeps the band narrow in the tails where a Kolmogorov–Smirnov band is too wide. The calibration assumes the reference family is right up to location and scale, which are estimated.

title: From the question to the model
text:
Three means, three questions



Table of the arithmetic, geometric, and harmonic means, with formulas and the inequality A at least G at least H.


Sharmi Murali: a sum, a product, or a reciprocal. \(A \ge G \ge H\) for positive numbers, with equality only when every value is the same. A product process wants \(G\), and logging \(Y\) changes the estimand to that mean.

Walk the three columns in the figure: sum, product, reciprocal. \(A \ge G \ge H\) is the inequality to remember. Link logging \(Y\) to the geometric mean and forward to the log-estimand slide—students often report \(A\) after a log transform.
Going further. \(A \ge G\) is Jensen’s inequality for the concave \(\log\): \(\overline{\log x} \le \log \bar{x}\). For a log-normal \(Y\) with \(\log Y \sim \mathcal{N}(m, s^2)\), the geometric mean is \(e^{m}\) (the median) and the arithmetic mean is \(e^{m + s^2/2}\), so the gap grows with the log-scale spread. \(G \ge H\) follows by applying \(A \ge G\) to the reciprocals.

title: From the question to the model
section: Show the difference, not a star
text:
Show the difference, not a star



Five panels from Ho and colleagues: a bar chart, a box plot, a scatter with means, a null distribution of the difference, and a Gardner–Altman plot of the mean difference with an interval.


Ho and colleagues. Panel e is the graphic this workshop keeps: \(\Delta\) and an interval.

Scan panels a–c as what not to stop at, then land on panel e: mean difference \(\Delta\) with an interval on a difference axis. Contrast with a lone star or \(p\)-value. This is the reporting standard the pitfalls section keeps returning to.

title: From the question to the model
text:
Four questions, not one test



Four cards: tests of whole distributions, stochastic superiority, specific features such as quantiles, and parametric parameters.


Olszewski groups comparisons of two or more samples by the question, from the most general to the most specific. About nine hundred named procedures sit in these groups. The name of the procedure is not the hypothesis.

Read the four cards left to right as increasing specificity. “Nine hundred” is Olszewski’s scale—use it to deflate test shopping. Ask which card a Mann–Whitney user actually picked (often not the one they think).

title: From the question to the model
section: A permutation \(p\) for the same Welch statistic
text:
A permutation \(p\) for the same Welch statistic
Olszewski: MKinfer::perm.t.test uses the Welch–Satterthwaite statistic unless you set var.equal = TRUE. Leave the default. Do not pretest the variances with an \(F\) test.

result <- MKinfer::perm.t.test(
  response ~ group, data = data, permStat = TRUE
)
MKinfer::h0plot(result)


The call returns the classical \(p\) and the permutation \(p\). Compare them, and look at the null distribution of the permuted statistic as well as the residual QQ plot. Use more than 9999 draws for a stable \(p\), and on the order of 50,000 if the level of interest is below 0.001. Record the seed. Permuting the raw difference of means quietly assumes equal variances. The studentized statistic is the one Janssen (1997) gives for unequal variances; he lists that paper under the post. A reported permutation \(p\) of exactly 0 is a convention about the draws, not a probability.
Going further. A permutation test is exact when the observations are exchangeable under the null; equal means with unequal variances do not give exchangeability. Chung and Romano (Annals of Statistics, 2013) show that permuting a studentised statistic gives a test that is exact under exchangeability and asymptotically valid under the weaker mean null, which is why the Welch statistic is the one to permute. With \(B\) random permutations, report \((1 + \#\{T^*_b \ge T\})/(1 + B)\), which is never 0 and keeps the test valid (Phipson and Smyth, Statistical Applications in Genetics and Molecular Biology, 2010).

title: From the question to the model
section: A bell curve is not a feature test
text:
A bell curve is not a feature test



Recovery rates piled against 100 percent, with a 1-sigma interval of 92 plus or minus 12 and a 2-sigma interval of 92 plus or minus 24, beside a normal bell marked 68, 95, and 99.7 percent.


Hartmann and Rudolph. The 2-sigma interval is 92 ± 24%, so it leaves 0–100. The bell beside it is the 68%, 95%, 99.7% picture. A normality test does not turn that interval into a recovery rate. The same objection applies to a concentration, a count, or a composition.

Point at the histogram piled at 100% and the 92 ± 24% band leaving the 0–100 scale. The bell’s 68/95/99.7 labels are the wrong feature for bounded recovery. A normality test on such data does not repair the interval—shape and support are separate failures.

title: From the question to the model
text:
Match the transform to \(v(\mu)\)
Huber, chapter 13, writes \(v(\mu)\) for the way the variance trends with the mean. Three prototypes cover most assays:

constant: \(v(\mu) = c\)
Poisson-like: \(v(\mu) = a\mu\)
quadratic: the standard deviation proportional to the mean, so \(v(\mu) = b\mu^2\)

A real measurement can add them. For microarray fluorescence he cites Rocke and Durbin (2001): background plus a multiplicative noise, \(v(\mu) = b\mu^2 + c\). A variance-stabilising transformation is built from that curve, so replicate spread no longer tracks the mean. One power for the whole sample, as on the Yeo–Johnson slide, does not use \(v(\mu)\).

Huber’s three prototypes—constant, Poisson-like \(a\mu\), quadratic \(b\mu^2\)—are the vocabulary. Rocke–Durbin adds \(b\mu^2+c\) as a realistic assay. Contrast VST built from \(v(\mu)\) with Yeo–Johnson chasing a bell shape for the whole column.
Going further. The delta method gives \(\operatorname{Var}\{f(Y)\} \approx f'(\mu)^2 v(\mu)\), so the stabilising choice solves \(f'(\mu) \propto v(\mu)^{-1/2}\), that is \(f(\mu) = \int^{\mu} v(t)^{-1/2}\, \mathrm{d}t\). Constant \(v\) gives the identity, \(v = a\mu\) gives \(\sqrt{\mu}\) (Anscombe’s \(\sqrt{Y + 3/8}\) refines it for Poisson counts), \(v = b\mu^2\) gives \(\log \mu\), and \(v = b\mu^2 + c\) gives an inverse hyperbolic sine, the generalised log of Huber and colleagues (Bioinformatics, 2002). The approximation is first order: it is poor for small counts, where the variance of \(f(Y)\) still depends on \(\mu\).

title: From the question to the model
section: A VST is for a Euclidean next step
text:
A VST is for a Euclidean next step
Reasons for analysing the transformed scale:

a plot, or a heatmap, that spends its ink across the range
PCA, or a clustering that uses correlation, no longer dominated by a few very large means
a method that assumes identical, homoskedastic noise

That is the machine-learning case: a method whose geometry is Euclidean and wants a roughly constant spread. The transformation is still a new response. Inference for \(\mu\) on the original support stays with the link.

Step the three fragments: heatmaps, PCA dominated by large means, homoskedastic noise for ML. VST is a preprocessing choice for geometry, not automatic inference on the original scale. The link at the end points to GLMs as the inference path.
Going further. DESeq2’s vst() integrates the fitted dispersion trend \(v(\mu) = \mu + \alpha(\mu)\mu^2\) of the negative binomial, and rlog() shrinks each gene’s log fold changes towards zero with an empirical prior (Love, Huber, and Anders, Genome Biology, 2014). Both are meant for distances, clustering, and plots; the differential test itself is done on the counts with the negative binomial likelihood. A Euclidean distance on the transformed scale is then close to a distance that gives each gene a comparable noise level.

title: From the question to the model
text:
Five count transforms









Transform
Equation
Suited to
Trade-off




VST
\(\mathrm{Var}\{f(Y)\} \approx c\)
PCA, heatmaps
✅ low counts · ❌ not a test of \(\mu\)


rlog

PCA, small \(n\)
✅ stable · ❌ can compress a real difference


\(\log_2(\mathrm{CPM}+c)\)
\(\log_2(10^6 Y/N + c)\)
a quick heatmap

voom

✅ models the spread · ❌ the weight is the point
