title: From the question to the model
section: A Wald interval is a large-sample interval for \(\pi\)
text:
A Wald interval is a large-sample interval for \(\pi\)


Burakov builds the interval for a new covariate row \(\mathbf{x}_0\) on the logit, then inverts it. The covariance of \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\) is \((\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{W}\mathbf{X})^{-1}\), with \(w_i = \hat\pi_i(1-\hat\pi_i)\).



\[
\mathbf{x}_0^{\top}\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
  \pm 1.96\sqrt{\mathbf{x}_0^{\top}\widehat{\mathrm{Cov}}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})\,\mathbf{x}_0}.
\]
The endpoints are symmetric on the logit. After the inverse logit they sit inside \((0,1)\) and they are not symmetric on the probability scale. The justification is the asymptotic normality of the maximum-likelihood estimator. A small sample, or the perfect separation on the checks figure, is outside that justification.

Build on logit with \((\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{W}\mathbf{X})^{-1}\); invert to \((0,1)\), asymmetric on \(\pi\). Separation and small \(n\) break asymptotics—link checks figure.
Going further. The interval is the delta method on the link scale, \(\mathrm{Var}(\mathbf{x}_0^{\top}\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}) = \mathbf{x}_0^{\top}\,\mathrm{Cov}(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta})\,\mathbf{x}_0\); inverting the endpoints is exact because the inverse logit is monotone, which is why the band is built on the logit rather than on \(\pi\). A profile-likelihood interval, the set of values whose likelihood-ratio statistic stays below the \(\chi^2_1\) quantile, is invariant to reparameterisation and behaves better in small samples; confint() on a glm returns it in R (the method moved from MASS into stats in R 4.4.0). Under separation the profile is flat on one side and the interval is half-infinite, which is honest; the Wald interval is finite and wrong. Pawitan’s In All Likelihood develops the comparison.

title: From the question to the model
section: A conformal interval uses a calibration set
text:
A conformal interval uses a calibration set
The same chapter then builds an interval whose coverage is finite-sample, under exchangeability, from a calibration set that was not used to fit \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\).

Fit the logit on the training rows.
On the calibration rows, score each residual. The Pearson form he uses is \((y - \hat\pi)/\sqrt{\hat\pi(1-\hat\pi)}\).
Add and subtract a quantile of those scores. On the logit scale the interval is symmetric around \(\mathrm{logit}(\hat\pi)\), and the inverse logit brings it back to \((0,1)\) without clipping.

A classical conformal prediction set for a binary label is a set of classes. The interval here is for \(\pi\). Whether the 0/1 outcome falls inside a narrow band for \(\pi\) is a different question, and he treats it as the wrong coverage check.

Step three fragments: train fit; calibration Pearson scores; symmetric band on logit then inverse logit. Coverage is for \(\pi\), not for whether 0/1 falls in band—Burakov’s distinction on slide.
Going further. Split conformal prediction guarantees \(\Pr\{Y_{n+1} \in C(\mathbf{x}_{n+1})\} \geq 1-\alpha\) in finite samples when calibration and test points are exchangeable, using the \(\lceil (n_{\text{cal}}+1)(1-\alpha)\rceil\)-th smallest calibration score (Vovk, Gammerman and Shafer, Algorithmic Learning in a Random World; Lei and colleagues, 2018, Journal of the American Statistical Association). The guarantee is marginal, averaged over \(\mathbf{x}\); coverage conditional on a given \(\mathbf{x}\) cannot be guaranteed distribution-free (Foygel Barber and colleagues, 2021, Information and Inference). For a binary label the conformal object is a set of classes, \(\{0\}\), \(\{1\}\) or \(\{0,1\}\); Angelopoulos and Bates’s A Gentle Introduction to Conformal Prediction is the accessible entry.

title: From the question to the model
text:
Ad hoc, post hoc, intrinsic
Qin Ma uses the three words for bioinformatics, and they transfer. An ad hoc analysis answers one question with one pre-chosen tool. A post hoc analysis, in that paper, reconciles several tools or several datasets after the fact. An intrinsic analysis builds the check into the model.
In this workshop “post hoc” also means the comparisons you make after a model that has more than two levels. Those are not the same operation. The next slides are the second meaning. Choosing the comparison because it was the significant one is data dredging: the hypothesis was suggested by the same data that are asked to confirm it.

Ma’s three words for omics; workshop “post hoc” also means planned contrasts after multi-level fit—disambiguate. Data dredging link when the contrast was suggested by the same data.

title: From the question to the model
section: A row of coefficients is a family
text:
A row of coefficients is a family


\[
H_{0j}: \beta_j = 0, \quad j = 1, \ldots, p.
\]
One row per coefficient hides that family. The matching statement is a joint region, or simultaneous intervals: Bonferroni intervals for a Bonferroni test, Tukey or Scheffé intervals for those contrast families. A logistic, Poisson, or negative-binomial model has the same family. The criterion does not change because the distribution did.




StatHarbor Analytics, Multiple Testing Correction (2026), from the slide “Multiplicity in Linear Models”. Testing and interval estimation are dual: a family-wise procedure induces simultaneous intervals with joint coverage at least \(1-\alpha\). Pointwise bands on a curve are the individual-test object; a simultaneous band is the corrected one.
Going further. Bonferroni controls the family-wise error rate at \(\alpha\) under any dependence, by the union bound; Holm’s step-down version (1979, Scandinavian Journal of Statistics) rejects at least as much with the same guarantee. Both are shortcuts of the closed-testing principle of Marcus, Peritz and Gabriel (1976, Biometrika): reject \(H_{0j}\) only when every intersection hypothesis that contains it is rejected at level \(\alpha\). For the coefficients of one fitted model, \(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}\) is approximately multivariate normal, so the exact critical value is a quantile of the maximum of correlated \(|z|\) statistics; Hothorn, Bretz and Westfall (2008, Biometrical Journal) implement this in multcomp::glht for lm, glm and mixed models alike (Bretz et al. 2016).

title: From the question to the model
section: A table of counts is a log-linear model
text:
A table of counts is a log-linear model
Penn State STAT 504, Lesson 10 models a contingency table by a Poisson GLM. The cell count is \(Y_{ab} \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(\mu_{ab})\). The lesson is this log-linear model. Independence, with neither margin as the response, is
\[
\log \mu_{ab} = \alpha + \alpha_a + \alpha_b.
\]

\(Y_{ab}\sim\mathrm{Poisson}(\mu_{ab})\); independence \(\log\mu_{ab}=\alpha+\alpha_a+\alpha_b\). PSU STAT 504 lesson—joint model, not logit of one margin.
Going further. Independent Poisson cell counts, conditioned on their total \(n\), are multinomial, and Birch (1963, Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B) showed that a Poisson log-linear model with an intercept gives the same maximum-likelihood fitted counts as the multinomial, or as product-multinomial sampling when the fixed margins are in the model. That is why a Poisson glm can fit a contingency table whatever the sampling plan. The residual deviance of the independence model is the likelihood-ratio \(G^2\) on \((A-1)(B-1)\) degrees of freedom for an \(A \times B\) table, asymptotically equivalent to Pearson’s \(X^2\). Bishop, Fienberg and Holland’s Discrete Multivariate Analysis develops the hierarchy of log-linear models.

title: From the question to the model
section: Smooth \(\mu(x)\), and say what you assumed
text:
Smooth \(\mu(x)\), and say what you assumed
StatHarbor Analytics, Smoothing and Nonparametric Methods, uses “nonparametric” for a curve that is not fixed in advance as a short formula. Complexity may grow with \(n\). The structure that replaces the formula is smoothness, locality, or a penalty.






Assumption


\[
Y = \mu(x) + \varepsilon, \qquad \mathbb{E}(\varepsilon \mid x) = 0.
\] The course notes write \(f(x)\) for this \(\mu(x)\). A straight line \(\mu(x) = \mathbf{x}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}\) is efficient when it is close to the curve, and biased when the curve bends.



Angelino and Marcone make the same opening: a linear model is easy to interpret, and the straight line is often an approximation.

Start in the assumption callout: \(\mu(x)\) is the object, not a transform of \(Y\). Point at the sentence about the straight line being efficient only when the truth is nearly linear. A common slip is to treat “nonparametric” as “no assumptions”; locality and smoothness are assumptions, just not a single global polynomial degree.

title: From the question to the model
text:
One path, rising flexibility





flowchart LR
  line["straight $$\mu$$"] --> local["LOESS"]
  local --> gcv["GCV"]
  gcv --> knots["knots"]
  knots --> penalty["penalty"]
  penalty --> gam["GAM"]






Left to right: a straight mean, a local polynomial, a bandwidth chosen by GCV, a spline with knots, a spline with a penalty, then one smooth per covariate.
Each step spends a tuning choice: a bandwidth, a set of knots, or a penalty. The last step is how that choice survives more than one covariate.

Walk the Mermaid arrow by arrow; pause on GCV as the first automatic knob, and on GAM as the escape from the curse of dimensionality. Ask which step first stops being a single formula you could write on one line. The map is the spine for the rest of the section.

title: From the question to the model
text:
Flexibility spends variance
At a point \(x_0\), the bias–variance decomposition for the curve is:
\[
\mathbb{E}\big(\hat\mu(x_0) - \mu(x_0)\big)^2
  = \mathrm{Var}\big(\hat\mu(x_0)\big)
  + \mathrm{Bias}\big(\hat\mu(x_0)\big)^2.
\]
Predicting a new \(Y\) adds \(\mathrm{Var}(\varepsilon \mid x_0)\) on top of that. More flexibility usually cuts the bias and raises the variance. A small bandwidth is the noisy end. A large bandwidth is the oversmoothed end.






Read the displayed decomposition at \(x_0\), then add verbally that irreducible \(\mathrm{Var}(\varepsilon \mid x)\) is extra when predicting \(Y\). Students often blame “overfitting” only on wiggly \(\hat\mu\) and forget the noise term. Tie “small \(h\)” and “large span” to the two ends of the trade-off named on the slide.
Going further. For a local linear smoother with bandwidth \(h\) and a twice-differentiable \(\mu\), the leading terms are \(\mathrm{Bias}\big(\hat\mu(x_0)\big) \approx \tfrac{1}{2}h^2\mu''(x_0)\int u^2K(u)\,\mathrm{d}u\) and \(\mathrm{Var}\big(\hat\mu(x_0)\big) \approx \sigma^2(x_0)\int K^2 / \big(n h f(x_0)\big)\), with \(f\) the design density. Balancing \(h^4\) against \(1/(nh)\) gives \(h_{\mathrm{opt}} \propto n^{-1/5}\) and a mean squared error of order \(n^{-4/5}\), slower than the \(n^{-1}\) of a correctly specified parametric model. The constant depends on the unknown \(\mu''\), which is why plug-in rules and cross-validation exist. The expansion assumes \(h \to 0\) and \(nh \to \infty\), an interior \(x_0\), and a smooth \(\mu\); it breaks at a boundary or a kink. Fan and Gijbels, Local Polynomial Modelling and Its Applications (1996), derive it in full.

title: From the question to the model
section: A kernel is a local bump
text:
A kernel is a local bump
Before the regression, the same idea estimates a density. Each observation contributes a bump of width \(h\):
\[
\hat f_h(x) = \frac{1}{nh}\sum_{i=1}^{n} K\!\left(\frac{x_i - x}{h}\right).
\]
They name four kernels: Gaussian, Epanechnikov, uniform, and triangular. Bandwidth matters far more than which of those four you pick.

For a Gaussian kernel, Silverman’s rule of thumb is \(\hat h \approx 1.06\,\hat\sigma\, n^{-1/5}\). They say it is often adequate for a roughly unimodal symmetric density, and that it fails for a skewed, multimodal, or heavy-tailed density. The AMISE-optimal bandwidth shrinks as \(n^{-1/5}\): nonparametric rates are slower than a well-specified parametric rate.
Going further. The asymptotic mean integrated squared error is \(\mathrm{AMISE}(h) = \frac{R(K)}{nh} + \frac{h^4}{4}\,\mu_2(K)^2\,R(f'')\), with \(R(g) = \int g^2\) and \(\mu_2(K) = \int u^2 K(u)\,\mathrm{d}u\). Minimising gives \(h^\ast = \big[R(K)/(\mu_2(K)^2 R(f'') n)\big]^{1/5}\); Silverman’s rule is this formula with a Gaussian \(f\) plugged into \(R(f'')\), which is exactly why it oversmooths a bimodal density. The Epanechnikov kernel minimises AMISE over kernels, but the Gaussian loses only about 5% efficiency, which is the formal reason the kernel choice is secondary. Data-driven alternatives are least-squares cross-validation (unbiased but highly variable) and the Sheather–Jones plug-in (bw.SJ() in R), usually the better default. Silverman, Density Estimation for Statistics and Data Analysis (1986), and Wand and Jones, Kernel Smoothing (1995), are the references.

title: From the question to the model
text:
Local weights for \(\mu(x_0)\)






Model


\[
\hat\mu(x_0) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} w_i(x_0)\, Y_i, \qquad \sum_i w_i(x_0) = 1.
\] Nadaraya–Watson sets \(w_i\) from \(K((x_i-x_0)/h)\). That fit is a local constant: a weighted average of nearby \(Y_i\).



Near the edge of \(x\) the window is one-sided, so a local constant is pulled inward and the curve flattens. That boundary bias is why the next fit is local linear.

In the model callout, emphasise \(\sum_i w_i(x_0)=1\) so \(\hat\mu\) is a convex combination of neighbours. At the boundary, name the flattening before students decide the biology “drops off”. The next slide is the fix: fit a line in the window instead of a constant.
Going further. Nadaraya–Watson is \(w_i(x_0) = K\big((x_i - x_0)/h\big) / \sum_k K\big((x_k - x_0)/h\big)\), the solution of a weighted least-squares fit of a constant. Its interior bias is \(h^2\mu_2(K)\big(\tfrac{1}{2}\mu''(x_0) + \mu'(x_0) f'(x_0)/f(x_0)\big)\): the second term, the design bias, depends on how the \(x_i\) are spread, not on the curve alone. At a boundary the bias is of order \(h\) rather than \(h^2\), because the one-sided window has a non-zero first moment. Both defects vanish for the local linear fit, which is “design-adaptive” in the sense of Fan (1992, Journal of the American Statistical Association, “Design-adaptive nonparametric regression”).

title: From the question to the model
section: Fit a line in the window
text:
Fit a line in the window


At \(x_0\), minimise the weighted residual sum of squares of a line in \((x_i - x_0)\). The fitted value is the local intercept.

Degree 0 is the local constant, Nadaraya–Watson.
Degree 1 is local linear. The usual default: less boundary bias, still local.
Degree 2 is local quadratic.

The SIB course LOESS often uses the quadratic. The two sources agree on the algorithm and differ on the default degree.




Step the three fragments: 0 recovers Nadaraya–Watson, 1 is the usual compromise, 2 is what LOESS may use. Ask why the fitted value is the intercept at \(x_0\) rather than the slope. Mention the SIB versus StatHarbor default only as a software detail, not a statistical fight.
Going further. Local polynomial regression of degree \(p\) solves \(\min_{\boldsymbol\beta} \sum_i K\big((x_i - x_0)/h\big)\big(Y_i - \sum_{r=0}^{p}\beta_r (x_i - x_0)^r\big)^2\), and \(r!\,\hat\beta_r\) estimates the \(r\)-th derivative \(\mu^{(r)}(x_0)\). Fan and Gijbels show that odd degrees are preferable: going from \(p\) even to \(p+1\) removes a bias term without increasing the asymptotic variance, so degree 1 beats degree 0 and degree 3 beats degree 2 for the curve itself. The fitted value is still linear in \(\mathbf{Y}\), \(\hat\mu(x_0) = \mathbf{e}_1^{\top}(\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{W}\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{W}\mathbf{Y}\), which is what lets GCV and effective degrees of freedom apply. Higher degree buys lower bias at the price of more variance in sparse regions, so a larger \(h\) is needed. Fan and Gijbels, Local Polynomial Modelling and Its Applications (1996), chapter 3.

title: From the question to the model
section: LOESS is that regression, with a span
text:
LOESS is that regression, with a span






Model


LOESS is local polynomial regression with a nearest-neighbour window. The span is a proportion of the sample, in \((0, 1]\). A typical example is \(0.3\). The window widens where \(x\) is sparse. The usual weight is the tricube kernel.




Choose the span, find the nearest neighbours, weight them, fit the local polynomial.
The fit does not start from a named formula, and it does not return one.
It wants a large, densely sampled \(x\). The usual use is exploratory smoothing of a scatterplot.


Contrast span \(0.3\) with a fixed \(h\): neighbours count, so sparse regions get a wider window. Fragment 2 is the honesty check—no single \(\beta_0+\beta_1 x\) to publish. Fragment 3 sets expectations: LOESS is for looking, not for a table of coefficients without extra work.
Going further. The tricube weight is \(W(u) = (1 - |u|^3)^3\) for \(|u| < 1\), with \(u\) the distance to \(x_0\) divided by the distance to the \(q\)-th nearest neighbour, \(q = \lceil \text{span} \times n \rceil\). A nearest-neighbour bandwidth is a variable bandwidth, \(h(x_0) \propto 1/f(x_0)\) roughly, so the variance is more even across \(x\) than with a fixed \(h\), at the cost of more bias where data are sparse. Because the fit is linear in \(\mathbf{Y}\), R’s loess() reports an “equivalent number of parameters” \(\mathrm{tr}(\mathbf{S})\) and approximate \(F\) tests between spans, but these rest on Gaussian errors and the approximation of Cleveland and Grosse. The method is from Cleveland (1979, Journal of the American Statistical Association, “Robust locally weighted regression and smoothing scatterplots”) and Cleveland and Devlin (1988, same journal).

title: From the question to the model
text:
Robust LOESS reweights large residuals
Robust LOESS protects the local fit from a few extreme \(Y_i\).

Fit an initial LOESS curve.
Compute residuals.
Downweight unusually large residuals.
Refit with both the proximity weights and those robustness weights.

The span is still chosen separately. The next slide is that choice, for a linear smoother. Robust weights take the fit outside the linear-smoother case their GCV formula assumes.

Walk the four fragments as an iteration students may not see in code. Stress that span tuning is separate from robust reweighting. Flag the last sentence: once robust weights enter, the neat \(\mathbf{S}\mathbf{Y}\) story on the GCV slide is only approximate.
Going further. Cleveland’s robustness step uses the bisquare weight \(\delta_i = B\big(e_i / (6\,\mathrm{MAD})\big)\) with \(B(u) = (1 - u^2)^2\) for \(|u| < 1\) and \(0\) otherwise, where \(e_i\) are the current residuals and MAD is their median absolute deviation. Two or three iterations are the default (lowess() uses iter = 3; loess(family = "symmetric") uses four). This is iteratively reweighted least squares for a local M-estimator, so a point with \(|e_i| > 6\,\mathrm{MAD}\) gets weight zero. The cost is that the smoother matrix now depends on \(\mathbf{Y}\), so trace-based degrees of freedom, GCV, and standard errors are approximations. Cleveland (1979, Journal of the American Statistical Association) is the original source.

title: From the question to the model
text:
GCV chooses the bandwidth


A linear smoother is \(\hat{\mathbf{Y}} = \mathbf{S}\mathbf{Y}\). Leave-one-out cross-validation refits \(n\) times. Generalised cross-validation approximates it:
\[
\mathrm{GCV}(h)
  = \frac{\frac{1}{n}\sum_i\big(Y_i - \hat\mu(x_i)\big)^2}{\big(1 - \mathrm{tr}(\mathbf{S})/n\big)^2}.
\]
The bandwidth that minimises GCV is their predictive choice. The same criterion, with the penalty weight in place of \(h\), is how they tune a smoothing spline. Kernel choice stays secondary.




Point at \(\mathrm{tr}(\mathbf{S})/n\) in the denominator as the complexity penalty. Ask what happens if \(h\) is so small that \(\hat\mu(x_i)\) nearly interpolates. Link forward to splines: \(\lambda\) replaces \(h\) in the same GCV pattern on a later slide.
Going further. For any linear smoother, leave-one-out needs no refitting: \(\mathrm{CV} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i \big((Y_i - \hat\mu(x_i))/(1 - S_{ii})\big)^2\). GCV replaces each \(S_{ii}\) by the average \(\mathrm{tr}(\mathbf{S})/n\), which makes the criterion invariant to rotations of the data and cheap to compute (Craven and Wahba, 1979, Numerische Mathematik, “Smoothing noisy data with spline functions”). It is asymptotically optimal for prediction error, but its curve is often flat near the minimum and it undersmooths in a noticeable fraction of samples, especially with autocorrelated errors, which it mistakes for signal. For penalised splines and GAMs, Wood (2011, Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B, “Fast stable restricted maximum likelihood and marginal likelihood estimation of semiparametric generalized linear models”) recommends REML for \(\lambda\) instead: it has a sharper optimum and less undersmoothing. For a non-Gaussian \(Y\), the residual sum of squares is replaced by the deviance (UBRE or GCV on the working model).

title: From the question to the model
section: A regression spline spends its flexibility at knots
text:
A regression spline spends its flexibility at knots






Model


Knots \(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_K\) cut \(x\) into intervals. A cubic piece is fitted in each, with \(f\), \(f'\), and \(f''\) continuous at the knots. The truncated-power basis is \(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \beta_2 x^2 + \beta_3 x^3 + \sum_k \theta_k (x-\xi_k)_+^3\).



The analyst chooses how many knots, and where. A common default is the quantiles of \(x\). After the continuity constraints, each added knot costs about one degree of freedom, and the spline is most flexible where the knots are dense. A step function, a piecewise constant, misses the trend unless the cut-points are real breaks. That is the dichotomisation case.

In the model callout, read the truncated-power basis once, then say software rarely uses it raw. Knot placement is a scientific choice disguised as a default quantile rule. The dichotomisation link is deliberate: cutting \(x\) is a spline with too few pieces and wrong continuity.
Going further. A cubic regression spline with \(K\) interior knots spans a linear space of dimension \(K + 4\), so once the basis is built the fit is ordinary least squares (or a GLM) and all the usual inference applies, conditional on the knots. That conditioning is the weakness: choosing \(K\) or the knot positions from the same data is model selection, and the reported intervals ignore it. Penalised regression splines resolve this by taking a generous basis (say 10–20 knots) and controlling wiggliness with a penalty instead of the knot count; Eilers and Marx (1996, Statistical Science, “Flexible smoothing with B-splines and penalties”) use a difference penalty on adjacent B-spline coefficients, the P-spline. With enough knots, the result is insensitive to their exact number. Ruppert, Wand and Carroll, Semiparametric Regression (2003), is the applied reference.

title: From the question to the model
text:
B-splines span the same curves
The truncated-power basis is clear and numerically unstable. A B-spline basis spans the same spline space with local support: each basis function is zero outside a few intervals. The design matrix is sparse, and the fit is better conditioned. Software prefers this basis. The knots are still chosen by hand. The next smoother removes that choice and penalises roughness instead.






Students who implement splines meet instability before they meet the maths. Local support means a knot move affects only a band of basis functions—good for interpretation and for sparse matrices. Hand-chosen knots remain; the penalty slide removes counting knots as the main tuning problem.
Going further. A cubic B-spline \(B_k(x)\) is non-zero on at most four adjacent knot intervals, non-negative, and the basis sums to one at every \(x\) (partition of unity); it is built by the Cox–de Boor recursion from piecewise constants. The truncated powers \((x - \xi_k)_+^3\) are almost collinear when knots are close, so \(\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{X}\) has a huge condition number; the B-spline basis spans exactly the same space with a banded \(\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{X}\), so the fitted curve is identical in exact arithmetic and much more stable in floating point. In R, splines::bs() gives this basis and splines::ns() the natural-spline version. De Boor, A Practical Guide to Splines (1978, revised 2001), is the standard reference.

title: From the question to the model
section: A penalty replaces the knot count
text:
A penalty replaces the knot count






Model


\[
\sum_{i=1}^{n}\big(Y_i - \mu(x_i)\big)^2
  + \lambda \int \big(\mu''(t)\big)^2\,\mathrm{d}t.
\] The first term is fidelity. The integral is curvature. Here \(\lambda\) is the penalty weight, not a Poisson rate and not a relative intensity. Large \(\lambda\) forces a smooth curve. Small \(\lambda\) allows a wiggly one. A straight line has \(\mu'' = 0\), so the penalty does not forbid a bend. It discourages a bend the data do not support.









Read \(\lambda\) carefully against Poisson notation from the previous chapter. Large \(\lambda\) shrinks curvature; small \(\lambda\) chases the data. The straight-line remark prevents the myth that penalised splines cannot be linear—they can, when the data justify it.
Going further. The penalty has a Bayesian reading. Writing the curve in a basis, \(\mu = \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta\), the penalty is \(\lambda\,\boldsymbol\beta^{\top}\boldsymbol\Omega\boldsymbol\beta\), and minimising the penalised criterion is the same as finding the posterior mode under the improper Gaussian prior \(\boldsymbol\beta \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \sigma^2 \boldsymbol\Omega^{-}/\lambda)\): \(\lambda\) is a ratio of noise variance to prior “wiggliness” variance. Kimeldorf and Wahba (1970, Annals of Mathematical Statistics) proved the smoothing spline is the posterior mean under an integrated Wiener-process prior, and Wahba (1983, Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B, “Bayesian confidence intervals for the cross-validated smoothing spline”) built the intervals mgcv still uses. The same equivalence writes the spline as a mixed model: the null space of the penalty (the straight line) is fixed, the penalised part is a random effect, and \(\lambda\) becomes a variance ratio that REML can estimate. That is the bridge to the design section’s variance components.

title: From the question to the model
section: The solution is a natural cubic spline
text:
The solution is a natural cubic spline






Theorem


The minimiser, over a suitable class of functions, is a natural cubic spline with a knot at every observed \(x_i\).



The same properties hold: piecewise cubic, knots at the distinct \(x_i\), continuous first and second derivatives, and linear beyond the extreme knots. An infinite-dimensional penalty problem becomes a finite spline. In matrix form it is penalised least squares, the ridge pattern \((\mathbf{N}^{\top}\mathbf{N} + \lambda\boldsymbol{\Omega})^{-1}\mathbf{N}^{\top}\mathbf{Y}\).
Effective degrees of freedom are \(\mathrm{tr}(\mathbf{S}_\lambda)\). As \(\lambda \to \infty\) the fit approaches a straight line. As \(\lambda \to 0\) it approaches interpolation. GCV, with \(\mathrm{tr}(\mathbf{S}_\lambda)\) in the denominator, chooses \(\lambda\).

The theorem is the bridge from calculus to computation: one knot per distinct \(x_i\), yet a finite solve. Walk \(\mathrm{tr}(\mathbf{S}_\lambda)\) as effective df and tie \(\lambda\to\infty\) and \(\lambda\to 0\) to the bias–variance slide. GCV reuses the same trace in the denominator as for kernel smoothers.
Going further. The theorem (Reinsch, 1967; stated in Green and Silverman, Nonparametric Regression and Generalized Linear Models, 1994, chapter 2) holds over the Sobolev space of functions with square-integrable second derivative, for at least three distinct \(x_i\). With \(\mathbf{S}_\lambda = \mathbf{N}(\mathbf{N}^{\top}\mathbf{N} + \lambda\boldsymbol\Omega)^{-1}\mathbf{N}^{\top}\), the Demmler–Reinsch eigen-decomposition gives \(\mathbf{S}_\lambda = \sum_k \mathbf{u}_k\mathbf{u}_k^{\top}/(1 + \lambda d_k)\), so \(\mathrm{edf} = \sum_k 1/(1 + \lambda d_k)\): each eigenvector is shrunk, the two with \(d_k = 0\) (constant and line) never, and the wiggliest the most. That is why edf is not an integer and why it lies between 2 and \(n\). Other definitions exist, \(2\,\mathrm{tr}(\mathbf{S}) - \mathrm{tr}(\mathbf{S}\mathbf{S}^{\top})\) for the residual degrees of freedom among them; they coincide for a projection and differ for a smoother. Hastie and Tibshirani, Generalized Additive Models (1990), chapter 3, compares them.

title: From the question to the model
section: Restricted cubics are the applied form of that constraint
text:
Restricted cubics are the applied form of that constraint
The BMJ guide calls the natural spline a restricted cubic spline: cubics between the inner knots, and a straight line before the first knot and after the last. The tails, where points are few and outliers bite, stay stable. With \(k\) knots the model spends \(k-1\) degrees of freedom. Three knots, their usual start, sit at the 10th, 50th, and 90th percentiles of \(x\). Three to five knots is the range they recommend, and AIC can choose the number. The exact quantile locations rarely change the curve.
Coefficients of a spline are not the summary. The partial-effect plot is.

Translate “natural” to straight tails beyond the outer knots—where extrapolation would otherwise explode. Three knots at 10th, 50th, 90th percentiles are a concrete default to quote. End on the BMJ line: report partial effects, not raw \(\theta_k\) from the basis.
Going further. Linearity beyond the boundary knots means \(\mu'' = \mu''' = 0\) there, which removes four parameters from the unrestricted cubic spline with \(k\) knots (\(k + 4\) parameters including the intercept), leaving \(k\), that is an intercept plus \(k - 1\) slopes. Stone and Koo (1985, Proceedings of the Berkeley Conference in Honor of Jerzy Neyman and Jack Kiefer) proposed the restriction; Harrell’s Regression Modeling Strategies (2nd edition, 2015, chapter 2) gives the default knot quantiles for \(k = 3\) to \(7\) and the rms::rcs() parametrisation. A test of linearity is the joint Wald or likelihood-ratio test that the \(k - 2\) non-linear coefficients are zero, and it is valid only if \(k\) was fixed before looking at the data. For a GLM the curve is linear on the link scale in the tails, not on the scale of \(Y\).

title: From the question to the model
text:
The curve can rise twice
On the meningitis data, CSF glucose against bacterial meningitis: a straight line, and a cut at 62 mg/dL, both miss the second rise at high glucose that the three-knot restricted cubic shows.






Assumption


Do not categorise a continuous covariate, and do not assume a straight line, whether the aim is to predict, explain, or describe. Spend degrees of freedom first on the covariates that matter. Choosing the shape by eye, before the fit, spends phantom degrees of freedom and makes the interval too narrow.









Point at 62 mg/dL as the failed dichotomy, then at the second rise only the spline catches. The assumption callout is the policy slide: eyeballing the shape before fitting steals df and narrows intervals dishonestly. About two minutes if you discuss phantom df.
Going further. “Phantom degrees of freedom” is Harrell’s name, in Regression Modeling Strategies, for the parameters a data-driven choice examined and then discarded: picking a cut-point, a transformation, or a knot count after looking at \(Y\). The final model reports only the survivors, so its residual variance, standard errors and \(P\) values are computed as if the shape had been fixed in advance; simulation shows type I error well above nominal. For an optimised cut-point the problem is classical: the minimum \(P\) value over cut-points needs a correction (Altman, Lausen, Sauerbrei and Schumacher, 1994, Journal of the National Cancer Institute, “Dangers of using ‘optimal’ cutpoints in the evaluation of prognostic factors”). The honest alternatives are to pre-specify the number of knots, to penalise and estimate \(\lambda\) as part of the fit, or to bootstrap the whole selection procedure.

title: From the question to the model
section: A neighbourhood empties as dimension grows
text:
A neighbourhood empties as dimension grows
Local methods need nearby observations. As the number of covariates grows, those neighbourhoods empty, and “local” stops meaning a small window. Naive multivariate smoothing breaks down. The practical compromise is an additive mean: one smooth per covariate, estimated as a one-dimensional problem.






Draw an empty ball in \(p\) dimensions with fixed neighbour count—intuition beats formula here. Additive structure is a modelling assumption, not a free lunch: no interactions unless you add them. The GAM slide is the constructive response named on this slide.
Going further. To capture a fraction \(r\) of uniformly spread data with a hypercube neighbourhood in \(p\) dimensions, the edge must be \(r^{1/p}\) of the range: 10% of the data needs 46% of each axis when \(p = 3\) and 79% when \(p = 10\), so “local” is no longer local. Stone (1982, Annals of Statistics, “Optimal global rates of convergence for nonparametric regression”) showed the best achievable rate for a twice-differentiable \(\mu\) is \(n^{-4/(4+p)}\) for the mean squared error, so the sample needed for a given accuracy grows exponentially in \(p\). An additive model restores the one-dimensional rate \(n^{-4/5}\) for each component, whatever \(p\), because each \(s_j\) is estimated from one coordinate. The price is bias whenever the true \(\mu\) has interactions, which can be added back as low-dimensional tensor-product smooths. Hastie, Tibshirani and Friedman, The Elements of Statistical Learning (2009), section 2.5, gives the geometry.

title: From the question to the model
section: A GAM is an additive smooth on the link
text:
A GAM is an additive smooth on the link






Model


\[
g(\mu) = \beta_0 + s_1(x_1) + \cdots + s_p(x_p),
\qquad \mu = \mathbb{E}(Y \mid \mathbf{x}).
\] A logistic GAM uses the logit. A Poisson GAM uses the log. Each \(s_j\) is a one-dimensional smoother. Backfitting cycles through partial residuals until the smooths settle.



Because the mean is a sum, each \(\hat s_j\) has its own plot: a line, a threshold, a saturation, a U-shape. That plot is the component, not a black-box importance score. The BMJ guide names mgcv for this fit, beside rms for the restricted cubic, and treats GAMs and LOESS as the alternatives to fractional polynomials and splines.

Read \(g(\mu)\) first so Poisson and logistic examples slot in from the GLM hour. Each \(\hat s_j\) plot is the estimand for that covariate, holding others in the partial-residual sense. Mention mgcv and rms as the two R cultures named on the slide.
Going further. Modern GAM software does not backfit: mgcv writes each \(s_j\) in a penalised regression-spline basis, absorbs an identifiability constraint \(\sum_i s_j(x_{ij}) = 0\), and maximises the penalised likelihood by penalised iteratively reweighted least squares, with the vector of smoothing parameters chosen by REML or marginal likelihood (Wood, Generalized Additive Models: An Introduction with R, 2nd edition, 2017). Pointwise intervals come from the Bayesian posterior covariance \((\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{W}\mathbf{X} + \mathbf{S}_\lambda)^{-1}\phi\), here with \(\mathbf{S}_\lambda\) the summed penalty matrices; Marra and Wood (2012, Scandinavian Journal of Statistics) show they have close to nominal coverage averaged across the function, not at every \(x\). The \(P\) values in summary.gam() are approximate Wald tests with a reference distribution on the edf (Wood, 2013, Biometrika, “On p-values for smooth components of an extended generalized additive model”) and ignore the uncertainty in \(\lambda\), so they tend to be somewhat too small. Concurvity, the smooth analogue of collinearity, arises when one \(s_j(x_j)\) can be well approximated by the others; mgcv::concurvity() reports it, and high values make each component unstable even when the sum is well estimated.

title: From the question to the model
text:
Which smoother for which task

Exploratory visualisation: LOESS.
Density estimation: kernel density estimation.
A stable smooth regression in one covariate: smoothing splines.
Moderate flexibility with the basis written down: regression splines, including restricted cubics and B-splines.
Several covariates, with a plot per covariate: a generalised additive model.


Step the five fragments and ask the room to match a CA-SYS or SPRUCE exploratory plot to item 1 versus item 5. KDE is easy to forget because regression stole the hour. Item 4 is when you need a written basis for simulation or reporting.

title: From the question to the model
text:
Four controls on the flexibility

Smoothness or locality replaces a rigid global formula.
The control is a bandwidth, a penalty, or the size of the basis.
Choosing that control is part of the performance, not a detail after the fit.
In higher dimensions, an additive structure, or some other structure, becomes necessary.







StatHarbor’s reading list: Hastie, Tibshirani, and Friedman (2009), The Elements of Statistical Learning; Wood (2017), Generalized Additive Models: An Introduction with R; Wasserman (2006), All of Nonparametric Statistics; Fan and Gijbels (1996), Local Polynomial Modelling and Its Applications; Silverman (1986), Density Estimation for Statistics and Data Analysis; Green and Silverman (1994), Nonparametric Regression and Generalized Linear Models. MARS and projection pursuit are their two extensions that relax strict additivity. They mark the links to kernels and neural nets as conceptual, not equivalences.

title: From the question to the model
section: A study leaves some conditions free
text:
A study leaves some conditions free
In a study, conditions that move the outcome are outside the investigator’s control. A field example is the weather, the food, and the predators.

In an observational study the variable of interest itself is not assigned. That is where the reminder sits: correlation is not causation.


Field weather is the uncontrolled nuisance example. Step the fragment: the exposure of interest is not assigned, so the causal section’s \(do(x)\) language matters later. SPRUCE is not this slide—it is closer to the controlled-experiment and trial pair.

title: From the question to the model
text:
A trial randomises the assignment
A randomised controlled trial still cannot hold every nuisance fixed. It does control who receives the intervention.

With a large enough sample, the nuisances average out, and the contrast can be read as an effect of that assignment.
The trial is prospective: the outcome is unknown when the groups are assigned.







Fragment one: randomisation controls assignment, not every nuisance. Fragment two: prospective timing—outcome unknown at allocation. Ask whether warming at SPRUCE is “assigned” in this sense (yes on enclosure). Bridge to the causal deck: randomisation is a design fact, not a covariate trick.
Going further. In potential-outcome notation, each unit has \(Y_i(1)\) and \(Y_i(0)\), and randomisation makes the assignment independent of both, so the difference of group means is unbiased for the average treatment effect without any model for the nuisances. “Average out” is a statement about the randomisation distribution, not about one realised allocation: a given trial can still be imbalanced on a covariate, and adjusting for a pre-specified prognostic covariate then gains precision without bias (Senn, 1994, Statistics in Medicine, “Testing for baseline balance in clinical trials”, argues against testing for imbalance instead). Fisher’s randomisation test uses the assignment mechanism itself as the reference distribution, so its validity needs no normality or independence assumption beyond the design. Imbens and Rubin, Causal Inference for Statistics, Social, and Biomedical Sciences (2015), chapters 5–7, develop the finite-population theory.

title: From the question to the model
text:
A meta-analysis studies the studies
Huber calls a meta-analysis an observational study of earlier experiments or studies. Two motives: a larger effective sample, and the hope that study-level bias averages out across studies.
The hierarchical version, one estimate per site, is fixed effect or random effects.

Meta-analysis is observational at study level: you did not randomise which papers exist. The two motives on the slide are sample size and hope that study-level bias averages out—say both, without overselling the second. Point to the link back to fixed versus random effects for “one estimate per site”.
Going further. With study estimates \(\hat\theta_j\) and within-study variances \(v_j\), the fixed-effect (common-effect) estimate is the inverse-variance mean \(\sum_j w_j\hat\theta_j / \sum_j w_j\) with \(w_j = 1/v_j\); the random-effects model adds \(\theta_j \sim \mathcal{N}(\theta, \tau^2)\) and uses \(w_j = 1/(v_j + \tau^2)\), which flattens the weights and widens the interval. DerSimonian and Laird (1986, Controlled Clinical Trials, “Meta-analysis in clinical trials”) give the moment estimator of \(\tau^2\); REML or Paule–Mandel estimators and the Hartung–Knapp–Sidik–Jonkman interval behave better when the number of studies is small. \(I^2\) describes the share of variability due to heterogeneity, not its size. Borenstein, Hedges, Higgins and Rothstein, Introduction to Meta-Analysis (2009), is the standard text.

title: From the question to the model
section: Twenty weighings are not ten people
text:
Twenty weighings are not ten people
Huber’s weight-loss question. Twenty weighings of one person, on a precise scale, remeasure a value you already know. Ten people, weighed once each, start to ask whether the effect travels.

Name the level you can generalise to: laboratory, operator, machine, protocol, strain, litter, animal. “Technical” and “biological” are too coarse for that list.







Huber’s twenty-versus-ten weighings is the memorable line. Step the fragment and make students pick a concrete level—sequencing run, core, plot—not the vague label “technical”. That list feeds directly into the replicate table for SPRUCE and CA-SYS.
Going further. With \(m\) technical measurements on each of \(J\) biological units, \(Y_{ij} = \mu + u_j + \varepsilon_{ij}\), the variance of the grand mean is \(\sigma_u^2/J + \sigma_\varepsilon^2/(Jm)\). Increasing \(m\) only shrinks the second term; when \(\sigma_u^2\) dominates, twenty weighings of one person leave the first term at \(\sigma_u^2/1\), which no amount of technical precision removes. The optimal split under a cost \(c_1\) per unit and \(c_2\) per measurement is \(m^\ast = \sqrt{(c_1/c_2)(\sigma_\varepsilon^2/\sigma_u^2)}\), the classical result for two-stage sampling (Cochran, Sampling Techniques, 1977, chapter 10). The level of inference is the level whose variance appears in the standard error: generalising to new animals needs \(\sigma_{\text{animal}}^2\) to be estimable, so at least two animals per treatment, and preferably many more.

title: From the question to the model
section: Randomise the nuisance you cannot block
text:
Randomise the nuisance you cannot block
When the nuisance is unknown in advance, randomisation is the practical strategy: at a large enough sample, its effect averages out. It also limits unconscious bias, such as extra care for the samples that were hard to obtain.
He points to Senn (2004) for the ways a “better” scheme than simple randomisation can go wrong.

When blocking is impossible, randomisation is the practical defence—both against unknown nuisances and unconscious handling bias. Mention Senn as the caution on fancy schemes without lecturing the chapter. Ask for one carbon-lab nuisance you could randomise but not block (plate position, run order).
Going further. Randomisation does two separate jobs. It removes systematic bias, because any unmeasured covariate is independent of treatment in expectation; and it justifies the error term, because under the randomisation the expected treatment mean square equals the residual mean square when there is no effect (Fisher, The Design of Experiments, 1935). Restricted randomisation (blocking, stratification, minimisation) keeps both properties only if the analysis includes the restriction, which is why a blocked design must have the block in the model. Run order and plate position are classic carriers of drift; a randomised order turns drift into noise, while a systematic order turns it into bias. Senn’s 2004 discussion of “better” allocation schemes (Statistics in Medicine) makes the point that deterministic balancing can break the link between design and analysis.

title: From the question to the model
text:
Balance makes each effect identifiable
A balanced design gives every factor combination the same number of replicates. Each factor’s effect can then be separated. A nuisance that is balanced against the factor of interest is in the same position.

An unbalanced plan can be forced by cost. The warning is that the analysis is then on thin ice.







Balanced means equal replication per combination so effects separate. Step the fragment: unbalanced designs are common when money runs out—keep the “thin ice” phrase for the methods section. Do not confuse balance with randomisation; you need both stories in different papers.
Going further. In a linear model \(\mathbb{E}(\mathbf{Y}) = \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta\), a linear function \(\mathbf{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol\beta\) is estimable when \(\mathbf{c}^{\top}\) lies in the row space of \(\mathbf{X}\); an empty cell, as in the right-hand grid, makes the corresponding interaction non-estimable. With equal replication the columns for different factors are orthogonal, so the sums of squares decompose uniquely and the order of terms does not matter. Unbalanced data break that orthogonality: sequential (type I), partial (type II) and marginal (type III) sums of squares then test different hypotheses, and type III tests on main effects in the presence of an interaction depend on the contrast coding. Searle, Linear Models for Unbalanced Data (1987), is the reference; Agresti covers estimability in Foundations of Linear and Generalized Linear Models (Agresti 2015).

title: From the question to the model
text:
A pair is one block



Left, treatment and control in one pot, assigned by a coin. Right, both plants on the same side, so the side is mixed up with the treatment.


The left pot is a pair: the nuisance (the pot) is shared, and the treatment is assigned inside it. The right pot lets the side of the pot wear the treatment’s name.

Cover the right pot first. Fisher’s complaint about Darwin was this picture: every cross-pollinated plant on one side. The coin is the randomisation inside the block. Thirty seconds, then the Huber link on the next slide.

title: From the question to the model
text:
Pairing is the smallest block
Block what you can, and randomise what you cannot. A paired design is the simplest block: twins, or the same person before and after.

Fisher criticised Darwin for putting every cross-pollinated plant on the same side of the pot. A coin flip for the side would have kept that side from masquerading as the cross.
When a natural pair does not exist, a matched design builds pairs on age, sex, or health, and treats one of the pair.


Fisher’s Darwin pot-side story is the vivid warning—blocking is about removing a directional nuisance. Fragment two: matched pairs when nature does not give you twins. Pairing is the smallest block; SPRUCE blocking discussion earlier is the same idea at enclosure scale.
Going further. For a paired comparison, \(\mathrm{Var}(\bar d) = 2\sigma^2(1 - \rho)/n\), where \(\rho\) is the within-pair correlation, against \(2\sigma^2/n\) for two independent groups of the same size. The relative efficiency of the paired design is therefore \(1/(1 - \rho)\): with \(\rho = 0.5\) pairing halves the number of units needed. The price is \(n - 1\) instead of \(2n - 2\) residual degrees of freedom, which matters only when \(n\) is very small or \(\rho\) is close to zero. More generally, the efficiency of a randomised complete block design relative to a completely randomised one is estimated from the block and residual mean squares (Cochran and Cox, Experimental Designs, 1957; Montgomery, Design and Analysis of Experiments, chapter 4). Matching without analysing the pairs throws the gain away, and for a binary \(Y\) the matched analysis (McNemar, conditional logistic) targets a conditional, not a marginal, odds ratio.

title: From the question to the model
text:
Ten minutes: name the units 📝
On your own study, or on SPRUCE or CA-SYS, write four lines:

the unit that received the treatment, or the exposure
the unit that was measured
what was assigned, blocked, or only observed
which rows are repeats of the same unit


Ten minutes, writing, not talking. If a group has no study of their own, send them to SPRUCE. Do not show the next slide until the time is up.

title: From the question to the model
text:
One reading: SPRUCE
SPRUCE is the designed case, so the words are easier to pin down than in an observational table.

Treatment unit: the enclosure. Warming and CO\(_2\) are assigned there
Measured unit: a depth on a date, inside that enclosure
Assigned: the ten chambered enclosures. Two ambient plots were never given a warming level
Repeats: depths and dates that share an enclosure are not new enclosures




If you need…
The replicate is…




The warming slope
The enclosure, \(n = 10\)


A collar method
Collars within an enclosure


A seasonal curve
Dates within an enclosure



The same table is where the replicate is. CA-SYS is the other exercise: the system sits on the plot, and the four points in a plot are the repeats.

Read the four bullets, then the table. \(n = 10\) is the line that surprises people who counted depth-date rows. Offer CA-SYS only if a group chose it: plot is \(j\), point is \(i\).

title: From the question to the model
text:
Treatment contrasts use one reference
Larmarange, chapter 26. For an unordered factor, R’s default is contr.treatment. A factor with \(n\) levels becomes \(n-1\) columns. The reference level sits in the intercept.
In the marker ~ grade example the intercept is \(1.0669\) and the grade II coefficient is \(-0.3864\). The mean at grade II is the sum:
\[
1.0669 + (-0.3864) = 0.6805.
\]
contr.treatment(n, base =) and contr.SAS() move which level is the reference.






Walk the arithmetic on the slide: intercept \(1.0669\) plus grade II coefficient \(-0.3864\) gives \(0.6805\). Emphasise \(n-1\) columns and one reference in the intercept. Students confuse “coefficient for II” with “mean at II” unless you do the sum aloud. contr.treatment and contr.SAS only move the reference level.
Going further. A factor with \(L\) levels and an intercept gives a cell-means model \(\mu_\ell\) with only \(L\) estimable means but \(L + 1\) parameters in the overparametrised form \(\beta_0 + \alpha_\ell\); a contrast coding is a choice of \(L - 1\) columns that removes the redundancy. The coding matrix \(\mathbf{C}\) (what contrasts() shows) is not the hypothesis matrix: the coefficients estimate the rows of the generalised inverse of \([\mathbf{1}\;\mathbf{C}]\), so reading a coefficient requires inverting the coding (Schad, Vasishth, Hohenstein and Kliegl, 2020, Journal of Memory and Language, “How to capitalize on a priori contrasts in linear (mixed) models: a tutorial”). With treatment coding the hypothesis matrix is simple, \(\beta_\ell = \mu_\ell - \mu_1\), which is why it reads well. In a model with an interaction, the “main effect” of another factor under treatment coding is its effect at the reference level only, a frequent misreading of type III tables. Any estimable contrast \(\sum_\ell c_\ell\mu_\ell\) with \(\sum_\ell c_\ell = 0\) can be obtained afterwards from any coding, for example with emmeans.

title: From the question to the model
section: Sum contrasts use the mean of the level means
text:
Sum contrasts use the mean of the level means
contr.sum compares each level with the unweighted mean of the level means. The last level is coded \(-1\), so one factor’s coefficients sum to zero and the intercept is that grand mean.
The grade level that was coded \(-1\) has deviation \(-(0.1525 - 0.2339) = 0.0814\), which is also \(0.9958 - 0.9144\).
Fitted values, residual sum of squares, and AIC match the treatment-contrast fit. What changes is the reading of each coefficient.

contr.sum centres on the unweighted mean of level means; the \(-1\) coding line explains the \(0.0814\) deviation. Stress that predictions do not move—only the sentences attached to each \(\hat\beta\). Ask which contrast you would use if the scientific question is “grade II versus average grade”.
Going further. Sum coding gives \(\beta_0 = \frac{1}{L}\sum_\ell \mu_\ell\) and \(\beta_\ell = \mu_\ell - \beta_0\) for \(\ell < L\), with the last deviation recovered as \(-\sum_{\ell<L}\beta_\ell\). The grand mean is unweighted, so with unequal group sizes it differs from the overall sample mean of \(Y\); a weighted-effect coding exists when the population mean is the target. Sum coding matters most with interactions: centred codings make the main effects in a factorial model average effects over the other factor’s levels, which is what type III sums of squares assume, whereas treatment coding makes them simple effects at a reference level. The two parametrisations span the same column space, so fitted values, residuals and likelihood are identical, exactly as the slide says; only the hypotheses tested by individual coefficients change.

title: From the question to the model
section: An ordered factor can carry a trend
text:
An ordered factor can carry a trend
Further codings in the same chapter.

MASS::contr.sdif compares each level with the one before it. For grade, II minus I is \(-0.39\), the same gap as the treatment contrast against grade I.
contr.helmert compares each new level with the mean of the earlier levels. Keep it for a question that is exactly that comparison.
contr.poly is the default for an ordered factor. The columns are a linear, a quadratic, and a cubic trend. That is the coding for ordered time or dose when the question is the shape, including a bend. The intercept is again the mean of the level means.


Step three fragments in order: successive differences (contr.sdif), Helmert versus earlier mean, then polynomial trends for ordered dose or time. Tie contr.sdif’s \(-0.39\) back to the treatment contrast against grade I. Pick the coding to match the estimand, not R’s default habit.
Going further. contr.poly returns orthogonal polynomial contrasts: for \(L\) equally spaced levels, columns of degree \(1\) to \(L - 1\), each orthogonal to the others and to the intercept, scaled to unit length. With balanced data the linear, quadratic and cubic sums of squares then partition the factor’s sum of squares exactly, so a lack-of-fit test of linearity is the joint test of the degree-2-and-higher columns. The default assumes equal spacing; for unequally spaced doses pass the actual values, contr.poly(L, scores = ...), or the trend coefficients describe the wrong shape. Helmert contrasts are also mutually orthogonal under balance, but successive differences are not, so their coefficients are correlated. Because a coefficient’s meaning depends on scaling, report the fitted level means or the trend in units of \(x\) rather than the raw .L and .Q coefficients.

title: From the question to the model
text:
Eight minutes: which contrast? 📝
Pick one factor in your study, or system in CA-SYS, or warming in SPRUCE.

How many levels?
What is the reference, if there is one?
Is the question “each level against a baseline”, “each level against the mean”, or “the shape along an order”?







Eight minutes. The next slide is the CA-SYS reading. Do not hint at contr.sum until they have written a question in words.

title: From the question to the model
text:
One reading: CA-SYS systems
system has four levels, SD1, SD2, TS1, TS2. They are not an order.

Against a baseline, SD1 in the intercept: three coefficients, SD2, TS1, and TS2. That is contr.treatment
Against the mean of the four systems: contr.sum. The coefficients add to zero
Tillage, no-till against tilled, is a different contrast. It collapses SD1 with SD2, and TS1 with TS2. It is not one of the three system coefficients

Warming at SPRUCE is the ordered case: five steps, so a linear trend is the first column of contr.poly. The system factor is the one that needs a reference chosen on purpose.

Do the SD1 arithmetic only if someone asks. The point is that “the TS2 coefficient” is not “the mean at TS2” until you add the intercept. Mention the SPRUCE polynomial in one sentence and stop.

title: From the question to the model
section: Do not bin the gradient you built
text:
Do not bin the gradient you built
SPRUCE kept five warming levels, \(+0\) to \(+9^\circ\mathrm{C}\) in steps of \(2.25^\circ\mathrm{C}\), each at ambient and elevated CO\(_2\), on ten enclosures.
A regression on that gradient was the design. Splitting it into “low” and “high” spends the shape the levels were built to show. The number of enclosures still has to exceed the number of parameters.






This is the slide the pitfalls section points at. Five levels are a regression, not a two-group test. Ten enclosures cannot carry a saturated \(5 \times 2\) cell-means model with a residual. One minute.
Going further. For a straight-line model, \(\mathrm{Var}(\hat\beta_1) = \sigma^2 / \sum_i (x_i - \bar x)^2\), so the slope uses every level’s distance from the mean; binning replaces \(x\) by a group indicator and, for a linear truth with evenly spread levels, loses a substantial share of that information (Cohen, 1983, Applied Psychological Measurement, “The cost of dichotomization”, shows that a median split of a normal \(x\) costs the equivalent of about 38% of the sample). The variance formula also says the D-optimal design for a known straight line puts half the units at each extreme; SPRUCE’s five equally spaced levels are a deliberate compromise that keeps the power to detect curvature. Ten enclosures leave \(10 - p\) residual degrees of freedom: intercept, slope, \(\mathrm{CO}_2\), and their product leave six, a saturated \(5 \times 2\) means model leaves none.

title: From the question to the model
section: Choose the runs before the measurements
text:
Choose the runs before the measurements
A design of experiments picks the combinations you will run, before any \(Y\) is recorded. The organising question is the objective, not the historical name of the matrix.
A smaller matrix buys its size by giving something up. The usual sacrifice is aliasing: two effects share one column, so the fit cannot tell them apart. The four families below are the ones the overview treats as the working set: fractional factorials, definitive screening, a response surface, and an optimal design.
NIST’s selection chapter is the map: how do you select an experimental design?

DOE chooses \(x\) combinations before any \(Y\) is measured—the objective drives the matrix, not the historical name. Aliasing is the price of a smaller design: two effects share a column. Name the four families on the slide as the working set for the next four slides, then point to NIST as the map.

title: From the question to the model
text:
A fraction spends the interactions


A full factorial of \(k\) two-level factors needs \(2^k\) runs. Ten factors need \(1024\). A fractional factorial keeps \(2^{k-p}\) runs. Five factors at a quarter fraction need \(2^{5-2} = 8\), against \(32\) for the full \(2^5\).
Resolution says which effects are aliased. A low resolution is a screen for main effects. A high resolution leaves the interactions you care about separable. NIST’s note on resolution is here.




Use the numbers on the slide: \(2^{5-2}=8\) runs versus \(32\) for a full \(2^5\). Resolution vocabulary tells you which interactions are sacrificed—low resolution screens mains; high resolution protects interactions you still need. Students sometimes treat a fraction as “the same factorial but cheaper” without reading the alias table.
Going further. A fraction is defined by generators: the half fraction of \(2^3\) in the sketch uses \(C = AB\), so the defining relation is \(I = ABC\) and every effect is aliased with its product with \(ABC\) (\(A\) with \(BC\), \(B\) with \(AC\), \(C\) with \(AB\)). The resolution is the length of the shortest word in the defining relation: resolution III aliases main effects with two-factor interactions, IV aliases main effects only with three-factor interactions but two-factor interactions with each other, and V keeps main effects and two-factor interactions clear of each other. Among designs of equal resolution, minimum aberration (Fries and Hunter, 1980, Technometrics) picks the one with the fewest short words. An aliased pair is estimated as a sum, so the fit is unbiased for that sum, not for either effect, and a fold-over can break the aliasing afterwards. Box, Hunter and Hunter, Statistics for Experimenters (2nd edition, 2005), chapters 5–6, is the classic treatment.

title: From the question to the model
section: A definitive screen also sees a curve
text:
A definitive screen also sees a curve
Plackett–Burman is the classical screen: \(11\) two-level factors in \(12\) runs, with main effects aliased with two-factor interactions. NIST describes it as a design for when the main effects are the focus.
A definitive screening design is the modern alternative for continuous factors. The run count is about \(2k+1\), so \(14\) factors need about \(29\) runs rather than \(2^{14}\). Each factor has levels \(-1\), \(0\), and \(+1\), so a quadratic term \(\beta_{11} x^2\) can be seen. JMP’s account: main effects are orthogonal to two-factor interactions, and those interactions are not completely aliased with each other. Definitive screening designs.

Contrast Plackett–Burman’s \(11\) factors in \(12\) runs with main effects aliased to two-factor interactions against definitive screening’s three levels per factor. The \(0\) level is what lets a quadratic \(\beta_{11}x^2\) appear—Plackett–Burman cannot do that. Quote \(2k+1\) when someone asks how many runs for fourteen factors.
Going further. Jones and Nachtsheim (2011, Journal of Quality Technology, “A class of three-level designs for definitive screening in the presence of second-order effects”) built the design from a conference matrix \(\mathbf{C}\): the runs are \(\mathbf{C}\), \(-\mathbf{C}\) and a centre run, which is why there are \(2k + 1\). The fold-over makes every main effect orthogonal to every two-factor interaction and to every quadratic term, so main-effect estimates are unbiased by any second-order effect. Quadratic terms are estimable, but with low power, and they are correlated with each other; a two-factor interaction is partially aliased with others rather than completely. Plackett–Burman designs (Plackett and Burman, 1946, Biometrika) have “complex aliasing” instead: each two-factor interaction is spread over several main-effect columns with coefficients like \(\pm 1/3\), which is harder to unpick than the clean aliasing of a regular fraction. Both rely on effect sparsity: only a few factors are active.

title: From the question to the model
text:
A surface needs three levels
Once a few factors remain, the question moves from “which factor?” to “where is the optimum?”. The working model is quadratic: a linear term, a square, and a product for each pair.

A central composite design is a factorial, plus axial points \((\pm\alpha, 0)\) and \((0, \pm\alpha)\), plus centre points.
A Box–Behnken design also estimates that quadratic surface, and it avoids the corner where every factor is at its extreme.

Both are in JMP’s introduction to DOE.

After screening, the question is “where is the optimum?”—hence linear, square, and product terms. Fragment one: central composite adds axial and centre points. Fragment two: Box–Behnken avoids the all-extremes corner. Both need more than two levels per factor; link back to SPRUCE’s continuous warming grid as a field analogue of “shape”, not necessarily a CCD.
Going further. The second-order model is \(\mu = \beta_0 + \sum_k \beta_k x_k + \sum_k \beta_{kk} x_k^2 + \sum_{k<l} \beta_{kl} x_k x_l\), and the stationary point is \(\mathbf{x}_s = -\tfrac{1}{2}\mathbf{B}^{-1}\mathbf{b}\), whose nature (maximum, minimum or saddle) is read from the eigenvalues of \(\mathbf{B}\) in canonical analysis. A central composite design is rotatable, so the prediction variance depends only on the distance from the centre, when \(\alpha = (n_F)^{1/4}\) with \(n_F\) the number of factorial points; \(\alpha = 1\) gives the face-centred version that stays inside the cube. Replicated centre points give a pure-error estimate and a test of curvature. The method goes back to Box and Wilson (1951, Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B, “On the experimental attainment of optimum conditions”); Myers, Montgomery and Anderson-Cook, Response Surface Methodology (4th edition, 2016), is the current text.

title: From the question to the model
section: An optimal design is computed for the constraint
text:
An optimal design is computed for the constraint
D-optimal, I-optimal, and A-optimal designs are algorithm-built matrices. They are the modern choice when the run budget is tight, the factors are a mix of continuous and categorical, or the experimental region is an awkward shape.
The matrix is less readable than a textbook factorial. The criterion is explicit: D-optimality, for example, targets the precision of the coefficient estimates. A mixture, where the factors are parts of a constant sum, needs its own geometry rather than one of these factorials.






When the region is awkward or the budget is tight, the computer builds the matrix against D-, I-, or A-optimality. Say explicitly that the criterion replaces the pretty symmetry of a textbook factorial. Mixture designs are the exception named on the slide—proportions summing to one are not a standard factorial cube.
Going further. For a linear model with design matrix \(\mathbf{X}\), \(\mathrm{Var}(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}) = \sigma^2(\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{X})^{-1}\). D-optimality maximises \(\det(\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{X})\), which minimises the volume of the joint confidence ellipsoid; A-optimality minimises \(\mathrm{tr}\big((\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{X})^{-1}\big)\), the average coefficient variance; I-optimality minimises the prediction variance averaged over the region, the natural choice when the aim is a response surface. The Kiefer–Wolfowitz equivalence theorem (1960, Canadian Journal of Mathematics) states that, for approximate designs, D-optimality and G-optimality (minimising the maximum prediction variance) coincide, and the maximum standardised prediction variance then equals the number of parameters \(p\), which gives a certificate of optimality. The criterion is optimal only for the model you specify: a D-optimal design for a straight line has no interior points and cannot detect curvature. For a GLM, \(\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{W}\mathbf{X}\) depends on the unknown \(\boldsymbol\beta\), so designs are locally optimal or Bayesian. Atkinson, Donev and Tobias, Optimum Experimental Designs, with SAS (2007), is the reference.

title: From the question to the model
section: A decision tree for the matrix
text:
A decision tree for the matrix

Objective, chosen before any measurement

Screen, when many factors might matter: a fractional factorial, Plackett–Burman, or a definitive screening design

Interactions, once a few factors remain: a full or high-resolution factorial

Optimise: a central composite, a Box–Behnken, or an optimal design


Taguchi, when the target is robustness to uncontrolled noise
Mixture, when the factors are parts of a constant sum



Walk the nested bullets top-down: objective before measurement, then screen versus optimise branches. Taguchi and mixture are leaves students may never use but should recognise on a methods form. This tree is the thirty-second recap before Schielzeth’s figures make crossing and nesting visual.

title: From the question to the model
text:
Eight minutes: name the plan 📝
For your study, or for SPRUCE, write which row of the map it is, and what the plan spent.

screen, factorial, gradient, or mixed model of units
what was given up: aliasing, a missing cross, or too few units for the parameters







Eight minutes. SPRUCE is the worked answer because the warming grid is a designed shape, not a screen of dozens of factors.

title: From the question to the model
text:
One reading: the SPRUCE grid
SPRUCE is not a fractional factorial. Two factors were built, and the combinations exist.

Warming is a gradient: five levels, used as a regression
CO\(_2\) is crossed with warming on the same enclosure
Ten enclosures. A slope, a CO\(_2\) shift, and their product are a few parameters. A separate mean for every cell is not
Nothing is aliased. The limit is \(n\), not resolution

CA-SYS is the other shape: systems sit in zones, and two zones contain only one practice. That is a missing cross, which is a design fact, not a fractional factorial you chose.

Count parameters on the board: intercept, warming slope, CO2, interaction, against ten enclosures. Then say the CA-SYS missing cross in one sentence. Do not open JMP.

title: From the question to the model
section: A random intercept is a distribution on \(u_j\)
text:
A random intercept is a distribution on \(u_j\)





flowchart LR
  mean["$$g(\mu_{ij}) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_j + u_j$$"]
  cluster["$$u_j \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_u^2)$$"]
  mean --> cluster






Use a Gaussian equation for \(Y_{ij}\) only when \(Y\) can live on that scale. For a count or a detection, the cluster term sits on the link, as in the diagram.
\(u_j\) is a property of the cluster. It is not a covariate you forgot to measure, unless you are willing to say so. Ignoring it is the pitfall repeated rows are not replicates.

Read the equation on the link scale in the diagram, not on the count scale unless \(Y\) is Gaussian. \(u_j \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_u^2)\) is a distribution over enclosures, not a missing fixed covariate. If someone proposes “just add enclosure as a factor”, ask whether they have all levels or a sample of bogs—that leads into the next slide’s columns.
Going further. For a Gaussian \(Y\), the random intercept induces a compound-symmetric covariance within a cluster: \(\mathrm{Var}(Y_{ij}) = \sigma_u^2 + \sigma_\varepsilon^2\) and \(\mathrm{Cov}(Y_{ij}, Y_{i'j}) = \sigma_u^2\), so the intraclass correlation is \(\rho = \sigma_u^2/(\sigma_u^2 + \sigma_\varepsilon^2)\). On a non-identity link the story changes: \(\beta_1\) in a generalised linear mixed model is a conditional (cluster-specific) effect, and the marginal, population-averaged effect is attenuated; for a logit link, roughly \(\beta_1/\sqrt{1 + 0.346\,\sigma_u^2}\) (Zeger, Liang and Albert, 1988, Biometrics). The likelihood integrates over \(u_j\), which has no closed form for non-Gaussian \(Y\); Laplace approximation (glmer() default) or adaptive Gauss–Hermite quadrature (nAGQ > 1) is needed, and both are less accurate with few observations per cluster. Testing \(\sigma_u^2 = 0\) puts the null on the boundary of the parameter space, so the likelihood-ratio statistic follows a 50:50 mixture of \(\chi^2_0\) and \(\chi^2_1\), not \(\chi^2_1\) (Self and Liang, 1987, Journal of the American Statistical Association).

title: From the question to the model
section: Fixed and random name the target
text:
Fixed and random name the target


Fixed
A contrast you want to report, such as the warming slope.
If you already have every level in the population, a fixed indicator for each level is coherent.

Random
A level you want to generalise over, such as enclosures drawn from a bog.
Ten enclosures is a small sample of a variance. \(\hat\sigma_u\) will be noisy.

Partial pooling is the practical reason to bother: an enclosure with two bad weeks borrows strength from the others. The meta-analysis version, one estimate per site, is fixed effect or random effects.

Left column: warming slope is a fixed estimand you report. Right column: enclosures are a random draw from a bog population, and ten of them makes \(\hat\sigma_u\) noisy—quote that line. Partial pooling is the punchline for sparse clusters. The meta-analysis slide, earlier in the hour, is the same idea with one estimate per site.
Going further. In the balanced Gaussian random-intercept model, the predicted cluster effect (the BLUP) is \(\hat u_j = \lambda_j(\bar Y_{\cdot j} - \hat\mu)\) with shrinkage factor \(\lambda_j = \sigma_u^2/(\sigma_u^2 + \sigma_\varepsilon^2/m_j)\): a cluster with few rows or noisy rows is pulled harder towards the grand mean. That is partial pooling between the two extremes, no pooling (a fixed effect per cluster, \(\lambda_j = 1\)) and complete pooling (ignore clusters, \(\lambda_j = 0\)). Robinson (1991, Statistical Science, “That BLUP is a good thing: the estimation of random effects”) reviews the theory, and Gelman and Hill, Data Analysis Using Regression and Multilevel/Hierarchical Models (2007), chapter 12, gives the applied reading. With ten clusters \(\hat\sigma_u^2\) is imprecise and can be estimated as zero, a singular fit, in which case the model reduces silently to complete pooling.

title: From the question to the model
section: Nesting is a property of the experiment
text:
Nesting is a property of the experiment
Schielzeth and Nakagawa (Methods in Ecology and Evolution, 2013). A nested factor can be fitted with the syntax of a crossed factor, provided each nested level has a unique label. The design still decides what the variances mean.
The difference that matters is the interaction variance. In a nested experiment it is pooled with the main-effect variance of the nested factor. A crossed experiment can separate the two. The pooling is fixed by which combinations occur, not by the formula.
If a cross would have been feasible and meaningful, the data are nested by design, and the pooling has to be stated. If a cross would be irrelevant, the nesting is natural.

Schielzeth and Nakagawa: unique labels let nested factors use crossed syntax, but the experiment still decides what variances mean. The interaction variance pools with the nested main effect in a nested design; a cross can separate them. Ask whether enclosure-by-collar should be crossed or nested given how SPRUCE was built—the Mermaid slide earlier is your answer key.
Going further. In a balanced two-way random model with \(a\) levels of \(A\), \(b\) of \(B\) and \(n\) replicates per cell, the expected mean squares are \(\mathbb{E}(\mathrm{MS}_A) = \sigma_\varepsilon^2 + n\sigma_{AB}^2 + bn\sigma_A^2\) and \(\mathbb{E}(\mathrm{MS}_{AB}) = \sigma_\varepsilon^2 + n\sigma_{AB}^2\), so \(\sigma_A^2\) is separable from \(\sigma_{AB}^2\) only because \(B\) is crossed with \(A\). If \(B\) is nested in \(A\), the corresponding mean square estimates \(\sigma_\varepsilon^2 + n(\sigma_{B}^2 + \sigma_{AB}^2)\): the two variances are confounded, which is the pooling Schielzeth and Nakagawa describe. In lme4 syntax, (1 | A/B) expands to (1 | A) + (1 | A:B), and (1 | A) + (1 | B) with uniquely labelled \(B\) levels fits the same model; the syntax cannot recover a variance the design never separated. Searle, Casella and McCulloch, Variance Components (1992), give the full derivations.

section: Four variances, if the design allows them
text:
Four variances, if the design allows them



Four sources of a trait value, and the four variances a crossed design can estimate. Schielzeth and Nakagawa, Figure 2.


A crossed design can estimate each of those four variances. Nested sampling leaves the interaction inside the nested factor’s variance.

Figure 2 flows from two factors and their interaction into trait value, then down to four variance components. In a cross you can estimate interaction variance separately; nested sampling pools it. Students often fit (1|nested) and interpret \(\sigma_u^2\) as “noise” without stating what was pooled.

section: ML and REML answer different targets
text:
ML and REML answer different targets
The practical gap is often small. A likelihood-ratio comparison of two models uses ML.








Question
ML
REML

✅ More accurate for the fixed part
Usable, and usually close

Switch to ML before the comparison


On a typical fit

The usual reporting fit



Angelino and Marcone, September 2026. Their general wisdom on ML and REML.









Use the rendered table: ML for comparing nested models by likelihood ratio; REML for variance components on a typical report. The row “Comparing two models” is the one students forget—switch to ML before the LRT. Angelino and Marcone are the source note at the bottom of the table.
Going further. For a Gaussian linear model with \(p\) fixed effects, ML gives \(\hat\sigma^2 = \mathrm{RSS}/n\), biased downward by the factor \((n - p)/n\) because it ignores the degrees of freedom spent on \(\boldsymbol\beta\); REML maximises the likelihood of \(n - p\) error contrasts \(\mathbf{K}^{\top}\mathbf{Y}\) with \(\mathbf{K}^{\top}\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{0}\), which do not depend on \(\boldsymbol\beta\), and recovers \(\mathrm{RSS}/(n - p)\) (Patterson and Thompson, 1971, Biometrika). In mixed models the same correction matters most when the number of clusters is small relative to the cluster-level fixed effects, exactly the SPRUCE case. Because the REML likelihood depends on \(\mathbf{X}\), two REML fits with different fixed effects are likelihoods of different data, so their ratio is meaningless; two REML fits with the same fixed part and different random parts can be compared. Harville (1977, Journal of the American Statistical Association) also gives the Bayesian reading: REML is the marginal likelihood after integrating \(\boldsymbol\beta\) out under a flat prior.

text:
nlme carries the residual correlation
The same course names two R packages. nlme is the one they single out for a flexible covariance. lme4 is the other. The split below is what the two fitting functions actually expose.
